Before the Orders of the Day are called, I would like to draw the attention of the Prime Minister to a statement which appears in this morning's * Citizen,' respecting the character and quality of the immigrants which are coming into this country. Statements of a similar kind have been appearing for the past ten days or two weeks in many of the newspapers published throughout the country. I draw the attention of the right hon. gentleman to this statement because appended to it is an explanation from the officers of the Immigration Department. With the permission of the House, I will read what the ' Citizen ' states. The item is as follows : STRANDED IMMIGRANTS.
Walking Streets of Montreal and Sleeping in Jails.	.
Dominion Immigration Agent says the Reuter Despatch is Exaggerated-Private Agencies Responsible for Evil that may Exist.
(Canadian Special Cable.)
London, May 30.-A Reuters' wire from Montreal states that thousands of lately arrived emigrants are walking the streets, and being sent to '.the j^ils for protection, and that railway cars are being used as places for shelter.
Courtenay and company, an organization for sending gentlemen as pupils to Canadian farms at a premium of 15 pounds each, has been using a circular quoting the names of Lord Roberts, Judges Sifton and Barrow and Governor Forget by way of certificates presumably 'testifying to the reliability of their work. Lord Roberts has interviewed Lord Strathcona in the matter, asking that his name be withdrawn.
That is the despatch. Appended to it Is the following statement:
The superintendent of immigration in this city, i interviewed concerning the above, said that the report in stating that ' thousands of lately-arrived emigrants were walking the streets of Montreal,' was undoubtedly exaggerated. iHe stated further that emigrants have been repeatedly warned against Courtenay '& Co., private emigrant agents, who do business at 2 and 3 West street, Finnsbury pavement, London, Eng. The Canadian immigration department, he added, frequently has trouble from a class of immigrants, with those coming to this country it has not been in any way identified. These are chiefly Galicians who book to Montreal, or some of the Atlantic seaports, and on disembarking have no money to provide for their transportation further west. They are often unable 'to find work ; but the department helping them as far as possible, is in no way responsible for them, or for any other emigrants who book to the seaports without provision for further transport, a pro-Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
ceeding against which emigrants are always cautioned.
The ' Citizen ' representative saw a number of Galicians on the stairway leading to the immigration offices, who looked very tired and hungry. They had come from Montreal.
It will be within the recollection of hon. gentlemen now present in the House that two or three weeks ago fifty Austrians reached this city in a state of semi-strava-tion, and wer* maintained by the Immigration Department until a few days ago. I am sure we entirely concur in the humane work of the Immigration Department in maintaining these people until some work could be provided, but I think the primary obligation rests on the steamship company which dumped them in Montreal or some other seaport town. The United States law obliges the steamship company to make provision for destitute immigrants ; and when statements such as I have read are sent from Canada to the old country as to the condition of things in seaport towns like Montreal, I think all the powers that have been vested in the Immigration Department should be exercised and that the responsibility for the maintenance of these destitute immigrants should be placed squarely on the shoulders where it belongs, that is on the steamship company. I am sure that the Minister of Labour (Sir William Mulock) is aware of the fact that complaints have been made as to the methods adopted on the other side to send numbers of undesirable immigrants into this country, and as we have provision in our statutes for deporting undesirable pauper immigrants and for placing the responsibility for their maintenance while here on the steamship companies, I think that no time should be lost in putting the law fully into force so that complaints of this kind could not be repeated. The right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) is aware of course that we have the power to turn these people back, and in view of the explanation which the superintendent of immigration has given to the representative of the ' Citizen,' which is not in my judgment satisfactory, I have taken the opportunity of bringing this matter to the attention of the House. I therefore beg to move the adjournment of the House.

I would like to add a word to what has been said by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke). Some twelve or thirteen of these Austrians found their way to the town of Almonte, in my constituency a few days ago, and they are perfectly helpless so far as making their wants known or conversing with any person is concerned. I am told they are Austrians who had no means of support or of going any farther, and they are dependent on the charity of the people of Almonte for a place to sleep in and for food. I think it is very unreasonable that

a steamship company should be allowed to launch these people on the country without means of support or of going forward to their place of destination. I therefore hope that the government will take some steps to remedy evils of this kind.

I think the government is guilty of negligence in this matter and 1 venture to say a few words because 1 think the evil is likely to increase rapidly. We have in Montreal and in the surrounding municipalities at the present moment a very large number of these immigrants who are idle and have become a public charge. It is the duty of the government to come to the assistance of these strangers, and to protect the people of Montreal from the charge for their maintenance which has been unjustly inflicted upon them through the negligence of the government in not protecting us against pauper immigration. In the United States the laws, already stringent against such immigration are being enforced with more rigour. The American government have agents throughout Europe who make sure before people leave for the United States that they will be suitable immigrants. The confidential report made a year ago to the United States government, by their agent Mr. Maurice Brown who investigated the sources of this undesirable immigration, ought to be sufficient warning to the Minister of the Interior. He points out that in the south of Europe the large steamship companies including some Canadian companies, have unscrupulous men as agents who take from intending immigrants almost everything they possess, and it is shown that some of these agents, have because of their conduct, been sent to prison in Austria and elsewhere. These immigrants are sent to Antwerp and English ports, and they are set apart as being undesirable for the United States, some of them having distinctive marks upon their clothes for the purpose of identification so that they may be directed to Canadian ports. There is an inspection for disease in Canada, but there is no carrying out of the law that guards us against the immigration of people who are liable to become public charges. The construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific and other important works #wi 11 bring out here a very large number of these undesirable immigrants. Not only that, but they are brought out virtually in violation of the contract labour law, because these European agents get money from the immigrants, and give them assurances that they will obtain work on arriving in Canada. In many cases they are coming out under written contracts. Mr. Brown reports that these people are separated into small groups in Europe, in order that it may not be discovered that they are under contract to perform labour in America. Such people are now entering the Dominion of Canada in very large numbers, and they are a burden upon the people of Montreal. The member for Laval (Mr. Leonard) tells
me that some of them have got into his count}', and the probability is that they will invade the larger cities and their surroundings! The only remedy for that is, that the government shoufld properly enforce our laws not only in Canada, but at the ports of embarkation in Europe.

speakeroldname: Hon. CLIFFORD SIFTON (Minister of the Interior).
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Canadian government has no control whatever over what Courtney and Company or any other private agency may do in England.
Except as to the quality of the immigrants that are being sent out.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I will get to that in a minute. Any number of individuals may unite in England to engage in business there without being subject in any way to the control of the government of Canada.
But the American officers inspect these immigrants at the points of departure.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Wait until I get through. We have no control over these private agencies in England ; they are subject to the law of England and not to the law of Canada. We have no power to interfere* with the operations of English people who associate themselves together in England for the purpose of carrying on any business whether it be proper or improper. We have no authority to interfere with them in the use they may make of the names of any gentlemen in Canada. I have no hesitation in expressing my opinion, that so far as the Canadian gentlemen mentioned are concerned, they have said or done nothing which would authorize the use of their names in the manner in which they have apparently been used. I will take steps to have these gentlemen communicated with by telegram to ascertain whether they have allowed the use of their names in that way, and I shall give such publicity to the result as may be necessary for the purpose of counteracting the effort as far as possible. I desire to say further, that the officers of the department in England have done everything possible for the purpose of making it clear to intending immigrants, that these voluntary organizations are not reliable, and that people would not be safe in depending on them. Not only this, but our officers have been interviewed and they have issued statements for the express purpose of making it clear that these organizations were not endorsed by the government of Canada, and that intending immigrants would not be safe in accepting the representations made by them. My information is to the effect that a considerable number of mechanics have been sent from England by organizations such as that referred to in this newspaper, and that difficulty has arisen because it has been represented to these people that they could find work at their trades when they got here. That has not been encouraged ;

on the contrary it has been discouraged by officers of the department, and we are doing all we can to counteract the misrepresentations made in that way. Only yesterday I sent a cable to Lord Strathcona, setting out explicitly that in my judgment no immigrant should come to Canada unless he was either a farmer or intended to engage in farm labour, and that these were the two classes only that should be encouraged to come here.
That is the policy the department has followed, in making every possible effort to place these representations before the public in Great Britain and on the continent of Europe in such a way that no mistake can be made about them. With the exception of these mechanics who have come over on representations made apparently by private agencies, the only considerable number of people who might be regarded in any way as persons who ought not to have been encouraged to come are a collection of Italian navvies who were lately brought to the city of Montreal. These people, so far as information goes, came as the result of the work of some employment agencies. We have not been able to ascertain what agencies caused them to come; but it seems clear that notice was issued somewhere in Europe, which reached the knowledge of these people, and they were induced to come on vague reports that there was railway work in Canada on which they would be able to get employment. They were in the streets of Montreal, and the evil had arisen before any information had reached the department as' to what was going on. The question now arises as to what is to be done with them, and our officers are endeavouring to ascertain the best course to pursue; but we have not yet come to any conclusion in regard to it. I agree with my hon. friend us to the necessity of preventing the landing in Canada of any persons likely to become a charge on the public ; but my hon. friends themselves will see that while it is easy in general terms to demand the enforcement of the law, yet when it comes to the duty, of deciding between the man who comes here honestly for the purpose of engaging in labour as a farm labourer, who is a fit and proper person, whom we desire to have come, and for whom there is an opening, and the person who is not desirable, but who is likely to become a public charge it is a difficult and delicate duty to perform. All I can say is that we shall endeavour to have the inspection made as carefully as possible, and to enforce the law which requires steamship companies to re-transport persons brought here who are likely to become public charges. Respecting what my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has said, I fear that his remarks may give the House an incorrect impression in regard to the facts. There is practically no Mr. SIPTON.
continued immigration to Canada at the present time from Italy. The particular people stranded in Montreal at the present time are of a class known as Italian navvies. Most of them have been in America before.
What about the Austrians who were brought out here two or three weeks ago ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where were they brought to ?
There were fifty of them at tne station here. Your officers said they would send the last of them away on Saturday.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Where did they go to V
I do not know.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The Prime Minister says he is tolerably certain that they were not Austrians, but Italians.
Twelve or thirteen of them came to Almonte.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I do not wish to be understood as saying that there were not forty or fifty people from any particular country. It is impossible for any one to speak with that degree of exactness ; but there is practically no immigration from Italy except that which was induced to come in the particular way referred to, and it is a special movement to which we shall give our special attention. As to the people who have come from southern Europe, apart from Italy, they have been, speaking generally, a good class of people, accustomed to agricultural operations, and they are now engaged either directly in agriculture on their own account or in farm labour. These people have practically all gone to the Northwest, and they are engaged there in useful occupations. So far as the general question is concerned, I can find no fault with the views expressed by my hon. friend. I agree as to the necessity of the most careful inspection to prevent the landing of undesirable immigrants where it can possibly be avoided.

I am prepared to give the names of the two agents in the south of Europe for lines coming to Canada, who are carrying .on this business contrary to the law and in a way that has been disapproved of by the inspector of the United States.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: I shall be glad to look into it.

Has the minister the authority to charge up against the steamship companies which bring out these unfortunate people the expense incurred by the department in maintaining them until it finds for them something to do ? If the

steamship companies were fined, they would be more careful about the class of immigrants they bring to our shores.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: They are liable to pay the expenses until the inspectors deport, and the cost of the deportation.

My hon. friend did not come to the point to which he said he would come, that is, the point mentioned by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) and my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk), who said that it was the practice of the United States government to send its agents across to Europe to make an inspection there of the immigrants who go on board steamships, and thus to ensure that no undesirable persons come over. When that was mentioned, my hon. friend proceeded to deal with something else and said he would come to it afterwards. It is quite true, we cannot control associations of people in England or anywhere else, but we can exercise control over steamship companies coming to our own shores. Our laws either extend to them or can be made to extend to them. Therefore if the Immigration Department of the United States can undertake that inspection on the other side and cure the evil where it begins, there seems to be no reason why our government could not do the same thing. I shall be glad for my own information if my hon. friend will give the reason why he thinks a similar course cannot be undertaken and carried out by this government.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: If I understand my hon. friend he refers to a proposed inspection at the port of embarkation of all the people who are coming to Canada and the furnishing of certificates from our officers there to those deemed of a fit class to come. I am not prepared to say that ought not to be done, but up to the present we have not found it necessary. If, however, my lien, friend is under the impression that there is a system of inspection by the United States officials of so effective n character that the United States are securing a more desirable class of immigration than we are, he is labouring under a most serious delusion. The average immigrant we are receiving is vastly superior to that which the United States receives. We are receiving at present, in the proportion of ninety-five out of every hundred, people who intend to engage in agriculture and who actually engage in agriculture when they arrive here. We can trace those people up and know exactly where they are and what they are doing. The United States, on the contrary, are receiving vast numbers from southern Europe, of people who are not of the agricultural class at all. but who simply go to swell, in many cases, the unemployed and the criminal classes in the large cities. And the American government have found it absolutely impossible to check to any great extent, this class who are merely labourers looking for odd jobs. The people we are receiving are of a very much better class, who become actual producers within a very short time. I do not say that it may not become necessary to make such an inspection as is suggested. That is a matter which has been under consideration during the last two or three months, more especially since the appointment of Dr. Bryce as medical inspector, but I have not yet come to the conclusion that it is necessary or desirable. It is quite possible, however, that the experience of this season may convince us that it is.

I think that this difficulty of a large number of immigrants overflowing Montreal and other places could be easily overcome, if they were the right class of people. There is room to-day for 50,000 men and women in the province of Ontario, if they are the right class, but it is little use to get people who do not speak our language and do not know how to work, especially people who have been living in large cities and towns, such as mechanics and that class. It would be very difficult for the farmers of Ontario to get along with them for a time. I think if the government had a railway of its own running into the Northwest, we could place these people on our trains and land them exactly where they would be required to settle up the country. I do not want to make a point against the government now for not building this railway and owning it themselves, but I want to say that the government could, with a stroke of the pen, If they liked, take all these people out of the large cities and leave them just where they are required. They can do it this afternoon if they like. I think that the trouble to which my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) has referred could be overcome if the matter were only taken up as it ought to be. The right way is to see that these people are distributed all over the country where required, and me Minister of the Interior is the right man to do it and to do it at once.

In addition to this matter of unuesirable immigration I want to bring to the attention of the minister the question of immigration under false pretenses of a large number of mechanics to the cities of this Dominion. Mechanics are now arriving at all our cities, more especially Toronto. Hamilton and Winnipeg, carrying with them what they believe to be a guarantee of employment. I shall just read an extract from the Winnipeg 'Free Press ' of last Wednesday, so that the House may understand the way this is carried on.
Among the immigrants to arrive in Winnipeg 'yesterday were a numberlof young Englishmen

who have been victimized by a lake labour bureau in London. They came to the west with the idea that situations were waiting lor them ,here and bringing what was supposed to be letters ol introduction ,to parties who would place them at work directly. On application at the address given there -was no work available and the London agent was unheard of. Several of them applied at the immigration department where steps are now being taken to block the scheme before any more victims are landed.
The scheme of the operation is to advertise that work of any kind can be secured in Canada for all applicants. The individual must pay his own fare to Winnipeg and must make a deposit of $5 as a guarantee of good faith. On calling at the office of the company or writing, the victim is told that an agent of the company will meet him at the dock with the necessary papers. At the dock he is handed a sealed envelope addressed to some one in Winnipeg, and which purports to be instructions for placing him in the desired situation. That is the last of it and when the dupe arrives in Winnipeg he is left entirely on his own resources.
That just outlines a few of the eases that occurred there on Wednesday. I have been getting a good deal of information regarding this matter. These immigration concerns are not confined to London at all but seem to extend all over Britain. Men are led to purchase steamship tickets on the understanding that they will be given a recommendation or guarantee of employment, so that they will he sure, immediately they arrive, of getting work. They are directed where to go. There is one feature about this business that deserves attention and that is that a great deal of the paper, on which the letters are written, is headed so as to lead those who receive the letters to suppose that they are official, and that they come from the Canadian government agents. There are joint letter headings useu by the steamship agents which indicate that they are also government immigration agents, and this leads these people to imagine that they are dealing with persons who are officially responsible. Young men arrive in Winnipeg without more than five dollars to spare and find themselves in a labour market which is absolutely congested and where there is no immediate prospect of their getting work. Thousands of them found themselves in that position within the last six weeks. A young man had a recommendation addressed to myself and another addressed to a contractor in Winnipeg. And when he presented his recommendation to the contractor, he found that 150 others had been there before him who had presented similar letters. I do not think it is necessary to go further in the matter just here, hut it is one of urgency. This is not a thing which occurred a few weeks ago and is over, but it is going on every day, and I believe is going on to-day in Britain, and I would suggest to the hon. minister that he should Mr. PUTTEE.
communicate with our High Commissioner ia London and have him bring the matter to the attention of the British government. Or. if not that-or, even in addition to that r-*the immigration agent of the government in England could meet some of the men who are returning with these guarantees and assist them to take action against the agents who are selling these tickets under false pretenses.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
Replying for a moment, and with the permission of the House, to my hon. friend, from Winnipeg (Mr. Puttee), X would say that the circumstances to which he has drawn attention are those to which I referred in my remarks a few moments ago. when I said that certain mechanics had come from Great Britain under representations which were not correct and that the disseminating of contradictions of such representations has been the subject of a good deal of effort on the part of the government officers. We have done absolutely everything it was possible for us to do to prevent these things from occurring. The facts to which my hon. friend from Winnipeg alludes were brought to my attention by a telegram from the superintendent of immigration in Winnipeg a few days ago. As I have said wTe are doing everything we can do to make known among intending immigrants the fact that these representations are not guaranteed by the Canadian government and that we do not regard them as reliable. In addition to this, our High Commissioner has been instructed by cable in regard to the facts, and, by this time, no doubt, has made a statement which will be thoroughly circulated in the English press.
Now, my hon. friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) has referred to a fact which, I think, is, perhaps, not sufficiently taken into account when the question of immigration is considered, that is the absolute dearth of farm labour in the province of Ontario, and the necessity of supplying it. I may say to my hon. friend that if the people of the province of Ontario could devise some means for distributing men whom the Department of Immigration could bring, this lack would be very 'largely supplied in a comparatively short time. It is most difficult, in fact, it is impossible, for the Department of the Interior to undertake the distribution of these men among the farmers. All that we can do is this, we can bring practically any number that may be desirable of good substantial men, men thoroughly qualified to do the work required-perhaps not expert farm labourers, for the supply of these is limited, hut men who would answer the purpose and whom the farmers would be glad to get. These men we could bring to a central point in Ontario, and if some provincial organization or method of distribution were provided I am satisfied that the wants of the
3S57

farmers of Ontario could be quickly supplied. I mention the fact so that it may be given publicity ; and for my part I should be pleased if the farmers' organization of Ontario, which have done such effective and admirable work, as, for instance, in bringing our friend from West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) into our councils in the House, would take the subject up and make a practical suggestion in connection with the distribution of these people.

If the plan of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) can be carried out, the hon. gentleman will confer a great benefit upon the farmers of Ontario. I can endorse heartily what has been said by the hon. member for West Elgin, that there is a demand in Ontario for at least 50,000 immigrants. I have had a good many applications made to myself personally and by letter and have generally had to turn them over to the department in Toronto. In my own constituency farmers are not able to get anything like the help they require. If I understood the Minister of the Interior aright he said that any number of men could be brought to a central point in Ontario. For two years, I have been trying to secure men for places in the county of Huron and I have not been able to get more than half a dozen. There is such a great demand for labour, the farmers are so anxious to get them, that, notwithstanding any difficulty they might experience with the lack of knowledge on the part of these men of our language, they would almost be glad to take even Italians or Chinamen, if they could not do better, and could get them to do the work.

Perhaps the hon. member for West Huron (Mr. Holmes) might think it well that the Minister of the Interior should send the two thousand Italians who have been dropped in Montreal in anticipation of getting work on the Grand Trunk Pacific. I think I see these men going into the agricultural districts of Ontario, and I can imagine how long the farmers of Ontario would put up with them. But I rose principally to draw attention to the fact that every year for three or four years past, complaints have been made of the arrival of undesirable immigrants in Canada, many of them diseased, some physically helpless and a large number of them paupers. And every time the matter has been referred to, the government has replied : There may be a few such immigrants, but we do not think there are many ; and in any case we will try to devise means to control this immigration as much as possible. And that is practically the reply that the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Sifton) has made again today. But it seems to me that for some years past the aim of the government has been to show that a large number of people have 122
been coming into Canada regardless of their quality. You see It in all the government organs that so many thousand have landed in Montreal, so many thousand in Halifax, and so many thousand have come in during the year. And all this notwithstanding the fact, which must be manifest to every one in our large cities, that there are collected in these centres of population many undesirable immigrants who are largely supported by charity. And, if they are not brought in under government auspices, at least they are brought in by reason of the fact that the government does not put sufficient restrictions upon their incoming. The Americans are trying to exclude this class of immigration, and they are doing it more effectively than we are. Why cannot we take a leaf out of their book ? Last year, or the year before, when statements were read in this House showing what the Americans were doing in this respect, the answer given by the government was that we in Canada did not need to take such precautions. But they agreed to appoint an inspector, and he has been appointed-inspector of health, I think thy call him-in the person of Dr. Bryce. The minister told us that Dr. Bryce had been appointed and that the government would consider what further was to be done. But, ever since last year, they have been merely considering the matter, and nothing has been done. Surely, with the influx of immigration into this country a large number of whom are undesirable, it is most important that the government should act promptly to check the influx of these undesirable people, before that influx becomes so extensive that it is impossible to deal with it. The hon. minister says that if the people of Ontario would take the immigrants he could supply and distribute them to the farmers, the wants of the Ontario farmers could soon be met. I ask him, what use, for instance, would be the Italians who were recently landed in Montreal if they were distributed among the farmers of Ontario ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is not justified in the argument he is making. I distinctly stated, that, as a result of the operations of some employment agency, these Italian navvies had been brought to Montreal. But I did not include them in the other remarks I made on the subject. On the contrary, I said that it was undesirable and a misfortune that they should be brought here. Everybody who knows anything about that class of people knows that they would not engage in farm work and would be very undesirable people to have on farms.

It is true that when the minister first rose he referred to these Italians. But when he spoke in answer to the hon. member for West Elgin (Mr. Robinson) he said that if the farmers would take the immigrants that his department could bring



11
into this country and distribute them he could supply the demand. That was a general statement regarding the immigration and would apply to these as well as any other class, and therefore I have a right to refer to them. How far is the government responsible for the coming of these people ? What do they cotne for ? To work upon the government's railway. That is the statement made in the Montreal newspapers-that they come here because they understood the government were building a railway and there was employment for any number of them if they were brought here. 'Who is to prevent them from landing if they are undesirable ? Is it not the government ? And yet the government seem to be remiss in their duty. Now what we complain of is that the government are not doing what they should do, and what they have the power to do, that is, to prevent these undesirable people from being landed in the country, people that are becoming a burden upon the charity of the country in such large numbers as at the present time.

Speaking as a farmer in the county which I have the honour to represent, I know that it is almost impossible to get any farm help. I was down to the Department of the Interior and spoke to the minister the other night. I would suggest to him now that he adopts some means of communicating with the farmers, surely he must have officials in his department who could communicate with the farmers, and ascertain their wants in this respect ; and instead of sending these men up to Toronto or some place further west, have them distributed where they are needed. I think he should let that fact be known, and appoint certain officials of his department to communicate with the farmers and send these labourers where they are required. I know a farmer in the township of Seymour, who has a splendid farm. When I was at Campbellford he told me he wanted me to call upon him. Now to show the minister to what straits the farmers are put in connection with farm help, I will tell him what this man said to me. This was Mr. Hugh Ross, who has one of the most beautiful farms in East Northumberland. He has no sons of his own, and he told me he was so tired with hard work when I saw him that he could scarcely talk. He said several men could be employed there if the farmers could only get them. Now, I am sure, with all the officials the minister has at his hand, there should be some one in the city of Ottawa with whom the farmers may know that they can communicate when they want labourers, and this official should send them labourers to the nearest railway station where they are wanted. It would be sufficient if they were sent up to Brighton, or Campbellford, or any of those villages along the frontier. Let the farmers send in their applications and state what labour they re-Mr. SPROULE.
quire. So far as my knowledge goes, it is absurd to talk about Italians going among the farmers. Of what good would an Italian be if you cannot make him understand what you want him to do. As my hon. friend behind me says, after you have told them what you want them to do, they would not know how to do it. It is trouble enough to educate an English * speaking labourer to the habits of this country, without having to take the trouble to get an interpreter to communicate with foreigners. I am satisfied that hundreds of English speaking labourers could be employed in that section of the country at fair wages. I would suggest to the minister and to his officials not to promise them too high wages. If a man is not educated as an agriculturist he cannot expect to earn high wages until he has learned how to work ; and when that time comes, he can get good wages all through the province of Ontario, especially, in the part where I live.

It strikes me that whatever effort we may put forth in this country we can never assimilate an Italian labourer and make a farmer of him. The moment you land them in this country their natural proclivities lead them to gravitate towards the city. That has been the experience in the United States and it will be our experience here. The fewer men of this class we import to this country the better for Canada. If j;ou place these Italians among the farmers''of Ontario to-day they will not remain long, they will gravitate towards the cities, where they will meet their own kind. I do not think any expenditure to locate an ordinary Italian upon a farm will be attended with "beneficial results. The fewer of that class you bring into this country to compete in the labour markets of the cities and towns of Canada, the better for Canada. What we want in this country, and it is a paramount want, is to make farm life more attractive, so as to induce young farmers to remain on the farms. Already the attractions in the cites and towns are such that they are drawing from the farms the men who should remain on them ; and we cannot replace them with advantage, either with Italians or with any of that class of immigrants that come from southern Europe. In the United States the labourers who did the work in days gone by, the Irish and the Germans, are being displaced by Italians and Polacks, and nationalities of that kind. In the city of Brantford to-day we have hundreds of Polanders and Armenians who are working in our factories. They are industrious and frugal, but you cannot make farmers out of them; and I do not think it is in the interests of this country to expend our money and our energies in bringing people in here, that won't make good farmers.
Why does not the hon. gentleman give the farmers telephones at a cheap price 1
I have no objection.

I was not present when the debate opened, and I am not aware whether the Minister of the Interior has been made aware of the fact that immigrants from Europe, immigrants who have been described as the least desirable, are being brought from the continent to America at 810 a head less than British immigrants have to pay. Is the Minister of the Interior aware that the rates on steamers from continental ports to Canada and the United States are $10 a head less than they are from British ports ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: There have been some changes lately, but as to their exact nature I have not definite information yet. We have received reports that certain steamship companies intended to make certain changes in their rates, but what has actually been done we have no definite information yet. It lias been suggested that certain companies intended to make a rate from continental ports to United States ports, discriminating against Canada, in order to take continental immigrants to the United States instead of Canada.

At present, rates from certain United States ports and from eastern Canada to the Canadian Northwest, Are lower than the whole through rate from Europe. As the minister knows, the Douk-liobors are brought 500 miles to Odessa, in Russia, by rail, then from Odessa they are brought to Canada or the United States by steamer and landed on the banks of the north Saskatchewan river at $55 a head ; while Canadians from the province of Ontario and the maritime provinces cannot be landed there for any such sum.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The information in the possession of the Department of Immigration does not show that.

There is a difference of $10 per head in favour of the foreigner. Why does not the Department of the Interior make some arrangements with the Canadian Pacific Railway, or the Canadian Northern, and the steamship lines, so that for every settler they put down in the Northwest from the eastern provinces of Canada, they should get a rebate of $5 per head ?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman {Mr. Sam. Htighes) want me to answer his question now ? It is because every member representing a county in the province of Ontario, including the hon. gentleman no doubt, would vote against the government If we did so.

There are a hundred young farmers from my own county now on farms in the Northwest, most of them good Tories, I am in one sense sorry to say, and who have to that extent depleted the Tory vote in the county. But I have the satisfaction of believing that an equal number 1221
of Liberals will turn over and support me when the next election comes on. But I want to make this point clear in connection with immigration. There are in England hundreds and thousands and tens of thousands of men of British nationality, labourers of every description who are anxious to come to Canada. Why cannot the minister, in addition to the efforts that he is now putting forth in that regard,-and I am not finding fault with these efforts although I am a little sorry he did not start earlier and get the wave which is only now commencing started some years ago, endeavour to make the most of the opportunities presented to us and get these labourers out to this country.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: We are ; that is what we are doing.

HUGHEiS. I mean to go further. The minister knows that long years ago I made the proposition that every man coming to this country should be assisted. In some of the best counties in Ontario to-dav there are farmers worth $5,000, $10,000, $20,000 or more, who were assisted from their homes in England by parishes and by this country. They were sent out by their friends without a dollar. They have done well, and why cannot we now adopt the same policy ? These men are unable to pay their expenses and bring their families out here. Why cannot the minister develop a scheme-there is no man In this country more capable of doing it than he is-to bring in thousands and hundreds of thousands of the right type of men, and if necessary when we place them on their little homesteads, give them their homes, give them their outfit to commence farming, the advance to be repaid in a certain number of years ? There are thousands of honourably discharged British soldiers open for service throughout the length and breadth of the empire. These poor fellows have no .money to place themselves away off in our Northwest Territories, and why cannot the minister evolve some scheme to bring these men out here, even if it costs $100 or $200 apiece to put them on their farms ? Let that be repaid, as it could easily be repaid, after a certain period Place these men on the farms, and then in ten, fifteen or thirty years, if the country wants to fall back on men, they will have them, and not such a type of men as those whom we see the little Japs rolling over by the dozen every time they meet. We have in the British Islands tens of thousands of men anxious to come to this country. Why cannot they he brought 1

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: What my hon. friend (Mr. Hughes) has said involves a very large number of questions of policy, which I shall not undertake to discuss this afternoon. I shall defer anything I have to say on the subject until we are discussing the immigration estimates.

There are thousands of men of all kinds coming into the country, and I think it is in the public interest to try to employ these men and make good citizens of them. I think an effort should be made to furnish them with a certain amount of money for buildings, give them a certain amount of education in the language of this country and train them to work on the farm. It is said that the Italians are no good. I say they are good workmen if they are properly trained, and I notice that now, when the Canadian people have any large contracts in building sewers and building railways, &c., in swampy ground, the Italians are the only class who can be got to go into the soil and take out the wet soil and throw it on the bank to grade the roads. If these people were taken care of and educated, we could make good citizens of them. The people in this country very often send to an orphans' home to get a child to bring up, and such a child is very useful to them, but if these immigrants can be trained as well as the children taken from the orphans' home, they would become good citizens. Money thus spent would be better spent than by sending Canadians to other countries to advise people to come here, although when they come here they know not where to go.

Something has been said with regard to the quality of the immigrants coming into this country. I agree thoroughly with every one that we should have a superior class of immigrants if possible, but because a man unfortunately chances to be born poor, that is no guarantee that he will not make a good immigrant. Something has been said with reference to the Polanders. I wish to say that thirty years ago a large party of Polanders came to Renfrew. They were very poor, so poor that the women went out to the fields to glean after the harvesters and gather berries to earn their subsistence, while the men worked on the farms. What has been the result?' A large number of those immigrants who came originally never learned our language except in an imperfect way, but their sons and daughters did learn our language. They went out to work, and their descendants have become to-day some of the best farmers in Renfrew. They have become comparatively wealthy, and what is more, they have made some of the best citizens we have. When war broke out in South Africa it was the sons of these men who came to this country thirty years ago, who volunteered and fought on the battlefields of Africa in support of our honour and our integrity. In the township of Sherwood there are 500 or 600 of these Polanders who are settled on farms, and a more industrious and a more frugal set of people I never knew. They are among the best farmers we have. They raise as good grain, make as good butter, have as good cattle, Mr. SIFTON.
as any citizens we have there. I have a Polander in my employ who has worked for me for seventeen years, and I have never had a better man, and do not think I ever shall. As a matter of fact, the only way in which we can now distinguish the children of these Polanders from our own people is that perhaps they are better looking, better dressed, more thrifty and make better citizens than our own people do.
You are placed in a fortunate county.

I think it is a pity that every once in a while we must have a discussion in this House because of the class of immigrants that are being brought in. We have been discussing this question for years, and while they have been improving to some extent, I think the department is not at all exercising that supervision over the class of immigrants coming into this country that they should exercise. It is astounding to observe what the American people are doing, and to compare it with our immigration policy. Last year the' American people got nearly 1,000,000 immigrants, and yet they would not allow any person to enter their country who was likely to become a burden, who was diseased, or who was in any way not a desirable person to become a citizen of that country. Instead of making the effort to get all kinds of people, the United States seek quality instead of quantity. They have compelled the steamship companies to have their laws in the language of the country, printed in large letters, posted up in their offices in every port from which their steamships sail. They instruct their officers to have the attention of the immigrants called to these laws. Then it is a fineable offenca for any person to solicit a person to come as an immigrant to the United States. Immigrants have also to pass a rigid examination before they are allowed to sail for the United States, and when they land in the United States they must undergo another rigid examination. Beyond all this the United States to-day have on our shores 116 officers whose duty it is to see that no person enters the United States from this country who is not a desirable citizen, or is not likely to become a desirable citizen. On the other hand, we have a large number of immigration agents in every*country that will allow us to have them ; and not only that, but we are pursuing, in my judgment, the worst possible policy with reference to agents. We are giving agents a commission, and I will go into the effect of this system, I hope, more fully at a later stage. We are allowing them to send out to this country any kind of person they wish, and they are paid a commission if they only get the certificate. Now, take it in the United States I have it on good authority that commercial travellers and people who are coming to this country to carry on business can go

to an agent who is on commission in the United States and get a certificate. They can present this certificate to the railway office and get their ticket for a fare of a cent'a mile.
That certificate is sent to Montreal, it comes back to the Interior Department here, and the agent is paid three dollars for a man, two dollars for a woman and one dollar for a child. I believe we artgetting no value for that money, and that we might as well throw it away. I believe that a great many of the immigrants we are bringing to this country are not such as we will be proud of in the time to come. I call the attention of the Minister of the Interior to a statement in the morning * Citizen,' that 7,000 pauper children are to be sent from England to this country. 1 do not think that is desirable I have time and again said in this House, that we should look more to the quality than the quantity of the immigrants who come here, and I repeat that statement now. The hon. member for Hast Assini-boia (Mr. Douglas) speaking at a Patron picnic in Prince Edward county declared that he did not see why we should be very anxious to give our fertile lands of the west to the pauper population of Europe, and I quite agree with him. I would rather wait a little longer and have a better-class of settlers. I think they will come. The trouble with the United States now is that they are getting more immigrants than they want, and we unfortunately have been willing to take their overflow of rejected immigrants, and have allowed the bulk of them to stay at the various ports in Canada. That should be put a stop to at once.

I do not think the hon. Minister of the Interior has made the matter much better by suggesting that these people afflicted with dangerous or loathsome diseases came from the United States to

Canada without any difficulty, and then were prevented from returning to the United States by the officers at the border. If that is the condition of affairs, it seems to me that it should be remedied at once. Why should we permit persons afflicted with loathsome or dangerous diseases to come from the United States into Canada without restriction, and then have these very persons, when they seek to return to the United States, stopped at the border and forced to remain in Canada? That condition of affairs should have been stopped at once and stopped long ago, if it has been continuing any length of time. So far as the immigration to the Northwest Territories is concerned, none of us denies that a large body of the immigrants from foreign countries are very desirable settlers indeed-Icelanders, Norwegians, Swedes, Danes. Alennonites, Germans, and many other nationalities which I might enumerate. For my part, I am bound to say that when I visited the Northwest some eighteen months ago I was agreeably disappointed in what I heard and saw of the Galician settlers. speechtext: I had not been reading Conservative newspapers so much as listening to the hon. member for Alberta (Air. Oliver) in this House. That was the source of my information. I had listened to that hon. gentleman making three or four speeches in which he had decried these people very thoroughly. For that reason I went to the Northwest with a prejudice against them, but I came back with that prejudice entirely removed, because I found that the Galicians were making good settlers. Their children were going out to work, their girls were going into service and intermarrying with English settlers, and in the second or third generations they will probably hardly be distinguished from the ordinary English settlers. I do not think my hon. friend the Alinister of the Interior is quite at liberty to say that no mistake was made in the Northwest, because we had incidents last year, to which I need not particularly draw attention, which were not of a character to impress us favourably in regard to a certain class of the settlers. There were scenes enacted during certain pilgrimages which were not very creditable to the country or to the settlers themselves. They were certainly not very edifying, so far as we could judge from the printed and pictured accounts of them. Therefore, while I am free to concede that the principal body of the settlers in the Northwest are a good class, whether English-speaking or not, I think it is going a little too far to say that no mistake has been made.

Speaker, I can only make a few observations on what I have seen at the port of Halifax, which is one of the principal ports of entry for immigrants from the continent of Europe, though we have also a great many from the British Islands. speechtext: Representing, as I do, a farming constituency in western Ontario, and having heard the Minister of the Interior state that he had plenty of good English speaking immigrants coming to this country who could be distributed throughout western Ontario at almost any ' time, I would suggest that he should send out notices that these men will reach certain cities and towns in western Ontario at stated periods ; and if he will do this, I feel confident he will find room for 5,000 of them among the farmers of the western portion of our province. As we are all well aware, many of the young farmers of western Ontario have gone to the Northwest and left the farms to a certain extent without sufficient help. Consequently, I believe it is the duty of the Minister of the Interior to send into that country at an early date a large number of suitable immigrants.

It appears to me that the farmers of Ontario who require this labour should organize. Let the different counties and municipalities organize and send requisitions to the Minister of the Interior, who has just told us that he can supply an unlimited quantity of such labour. That would be the business way to go about it. The hon. gentleman who has just spoken has told us that in his section some 5,000 could be employed. I know that farm labour is very scarce. Though representing a Quebec constituency, I live in Ontario ; and while it is unfortunate that these people should have come to Montreal, it does not follow that, even if they are destitute now, they are not good material out of which to make good citizens. No doubt the government will look after them and see that they are placed in the near future at such occupations as they can fill, r know many people who came to Ottawa without any money and wrere looked upon by the farmers as unfit for employment, bud who now can be employed at any service, and many of whom have raised good families and are numbered among our best citizens. In the Ottawa Valley there is room for any quantity of labour-mechanics and farm labourers and labourers of all classes:	It is the duty of the country
to do the best it can for these people who have arrived in this destitute condition and are now seeking work in the city of Montreal. But there is plenty of room for them in Canada, and no doubt they will all find employment if properly looked after.

speechtext: May I ask the Minister of the Interior if when he spoke of being able to bring in an unlimited number of farm labourers he spoke of men from the British Islands or men from the continent of Europe ?

maintopic: REPORT OF IMMIGRANTS REFUSED ADMISSION FROM FOREIGN CONTIGUOUS TERRITORY TO THE UNITED STATES, UNDER THE PROVISIONS OF THE ALIEN CONTRACT LABOUR LAWS, AND THE LAWS REGULATING IMMIGRATION, FOR THE YEAR ENDING JUNE 30, 1903.
speechtext: What I said was that we could furnish practically any number that are likely to be required of men quite fit to do farm labour and who, in that labour, would be satisfactory. I do not mean by that that we could get any number of trained expert farm labourers in the sense in which my hon. friend (Mr. Bell) will understand the word. In the old country, especially in the north of England and Scotland, what is known as a farm labourer is a man who is trained to that, who has been all his life at it, has been bred at it. But the number of these men is limited, and I do not pretend that we can furnish that class. But we can furnish as many as will be required of men who will en gage in farm labour and will prove satisfactory men. During the last couple of months I have had farmers from Ontario in. my office discussing the question. They say they have had labourers from England who have not been on farms in the old country but who made satisfactory labourers. We can furnish as many of these as may be required, but there is great difficulty on account of the unsatisfactory method of distribution. If that difficulty is overcome we can meet the demand.

House went into committee to consider the following proposed resolution :
Resolved, that it is expedient to provide that the bounty authorized by chapter 31 of the statutes of 1903, may be paid on lead-bearing ores mined in Canada and delivered at a smelter in Canada, on or after July 1st, 1903.- Rt. Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright.

I may explain that the object of this measure is to correct an oversight in the Bill which was passed last session. It was supposed that it would come into force much earlier, than owing to the lateness of the session, it really did. It was expected to come into force about 1st July, but did not come into force until 24th October. It was intended that the bounty should be paid on these lead-bearing ores on and from 1st July, instead of 24th October.
The Bill will have no effect except to fix the date at 1st July ?
That is all the effect it is expected to have. Of course, the Bill will be placed in the hands of hon. gentlemen in due course.
Was anything paid under the operation of this Act during the course of the last fiscal year ?
Not during the course of the last fiscal year because the Bill only came into force about the end of last October. Of course, a good deal has been paid during the present fiscal year.
I suppose the right hon. gentleman (Sir Richard Cartwright) is not prepared with a statement as to that at present ?
I can get the figures shortly. The amount has been very considerable-I. think about $70,000 or $80,000. A good many claims are coming in all the time.
Is the right hon. gentleman prepared to tell us what effect if any, the granting of the bounty has had on this industry in the province of British Columbia ?

So far as I am advised, it has had considerable effect, chiefly in the way of encouraging mining in certain classes of ores. It did r.ot receive sanction until 24th of October, and the effect has not been as great as it otherwise would.

I would like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether he has any comparative figures as to the production in the province of British Columbia during the time it has been :n operation, that is, the production for any month since the 24th of October as compared with similar months in previous years ?
I think there is some information of that character.

Perhaps the minister would be good enough to furnish ns with that information when he brings down the Bill.
Resolution reported, read the second time and agreed to.
