Bill (No. 113) respecting the Inspection of Grain (Sir Richard Cartwright) was read the second time.

I propose to refer this Bill to a special committee. The subject is somewhat complicated, and needs to be carefully considered. I move that the Bill be referred to a'special committee to be composed of Messrs Campbell, Ross (Ontario), Sifton, Douglas, Bickerdlke, Talbot, Scott, Henderson, Smith (Wentworth), Wilson and Robinson (West Elgin), the latter as representing the third party.
I would ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if an opportunity will be given to the grain buyers to be represented before the committee?
The committee is for that purpose. I refer the Bill to a special committee, so that all parties may be heard.
No doubt this is a very wise course, but it is unusual. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will be good enough to explain the reasons.

Most of the clauses of this Bill are by no means new. From time to time there have been many amendments introduced in the general Inspection Act, affecting the inspection of grain, and there has been a good deal of difficulty in ascertaining their precise meaning. The hon. gentleman will easily under-

stand that when a series of amendments are introduced over a considerable number of years they are apt to appear at any rate, conflicting with each other. The principal object I have in view, besides revising one or two important details, is to consolidate these amendments into one Act affecting this subject which everybody can understand. In addition to that, many complaints have been made to the department touching the inspection of grain. The hon. gentleman will understand that it is a matter of first rate importance that our inspection of grain, when the grain reaches the other side, should be maintained. I desire as far as possible to see to it that the inspection is made uniform, and that there should be no conflict between the certificates given by your inspector on this side and the condition of the grain when it is received on the other side. Also, I want, as fa*r as may be, to harmonize the rules which now subsist iu the two divisions. There are two great divisions, the eastern and the western, otherwise called the Manitoba. Now there has been a good deal of conflict of opinion between experts on this subject, and I think it would be highly desirable that all parties concerned should be heard before a special committee, who will give full time and attention to the subject. The officers of the department have bestowed a great deal of attention and pains in 'trying to make this Bill workable so far as they know how ; but of course their work will be none the worse by being scrutinized by a few other competent parties.

Iu view of the explanations of the minister, I think it would be a wise course to send the Bill to a special committee. The subject is a very important one. At the meeting of the Chambers of Commerce of the empire iu Montreal last year, some persons engaged in the grain trade found fault with the certificates issued.- I think the ;answer made was that the certificates complained of were really granted in the United States. But the subject is important, and I think it might very well go to a committee.
Motion agreed to.
Hon. RAYMOND PREFONTAINE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries) moved the second reading of Bill (No. 98) respecting the Harbour of Port Arthur.
What is the object of this Bill?

The effect of the Bill is to put the harbour at Port Arthur under the control of a board of harbour commissioners. A demand has been made by representatives in the county council and it has been thought that it was in the interest of navigation and of trade and
commerce that this could be done. There is a similar Bill as regards the harbour of Fort William. This was recommended especially by the Board of Trade of Fort William. It is an ordinary harbour board and its powers are more administrative than otherwise. They will have the administration of the harbour of Port Arthur but they will not have the right to borrow money.

Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into Committee thereon.	[DOT]
On section 1,
Is it usual in a place where there has been no local expenditure on a harbour to put that harbour under the control of the harbour board ?

The purport of the Bill, as I have explained, is to put the affairs of the port in the hands of a commission composed of men of the locality instead of leaving their administration in the hands of the Department of Marine and Fisheries as it is at present. The department of Marine and Fisheries now sees about the collection of dues, &'cr, and the Public Works Department sees about the construction of whatever works may be necessary. These two ports are becoming very important ; trade is increasing considerably and it has been represented by the people interested that by putting it into the hands of a commission in this manner the public interest would be better served.
Would it not be better served under qpe commission than under two ?.
There are two separate ports and they have asked that two commissions be appointed. Port Arthur and Fort William are not the same port.
Has there been a harbour-master at Port Arthur, and if so, what amount was collected by him from vessels last year ?
I have not that information under my hand, but I will obtain it.
Is it still the rule for the local harbour-master to collect from American vessels calling at Canadian ports ?

I cannot give the information now, but I will procure it.
On section 2,
What is it proposed to pay the harbour-master and commissioners ?

There is no salary as regards the harbour commissioners. If the commissioners appoint a harbour-master they will arrange that he should be paid by fees.

On section 5,
Do you give the commission charge of the government work there, such as the clock ?
The existing docks will be transferred for the purpose of administration to the commissioners who will also have charge of the docks that are now being constructed.
Is a record kept of the cash payments of dues, as there is a record kept of the tonnage ?
Yes, they are obliged to keep regular books and to render accounts.
Do they do that regularly ?
Yes.
Are the books audited and inspected ?
Yes.

We should so far as possible relieve transportation from all burdens, and I would not like to see this commission given power to impose larger duties upon the shipping interests than would be desirable. How do the rates in the past compare with the rates under this Bill ?

The rates fixed by the commissioners must be approved by the Governor in Council. The government would not allow any rates which would be detrimental to the port, nor can it be supposed that the local authorities would make any rates which would be against the interests of their harbours. In Montreal and other places the tendency is to reduce the rates. In Montreal the rates have been reduced fifty per cent during the last seven years.
What are the fees charged at present ?
I cannot remember, but there will be no increase under this Bill.
Are not the rates controlled by the department ?
Yes.
Then you should know what the fees are.
I cannot keep in my mind the fees charged at a thousand ports in Canada.
We don't expect you to, but when you bring a Bill here you ought to be able to explain it and not ask us to go it blind.
I will procure the information and give it to the hon. gentleman with great pleasure.

There is too much of this sort of thing ; ministers of the Crown bringing on measures and not being able to give a scintilla of information with regard to them. This is a very important step to take with regard to these hhrbours which are going to be great harbours. To my mind Fort William harbour is second to none in the Dominion. Before we pass a Bill giving the control of these harbours to three commissioners, we should know all details with respect to these harbours in the past, and their prospects for the future. It is all very well to say that the Privy Council will supervise these matters, but if the Governor in Council knows no more about it than the Minister of Marine does to-day, there will not be much gained by governmental supervision. The Minister of Marine seems to have been raking in from the other departments every power he can lay his hands on for his own aggrandizement, and although he has a great capacity for business, it seems to me that he has just got a little beyond his capacity. I would suggest to him that he should allow some of the other ministers to have a little bit of the administration of this country in their charge and not grasp the whole thing, and then he will be able to give information about the measures which he submits to the House. The Bill should stand until he is able to give the House the information.
I thank the hon. gentleman for the left handed compliments he has paid me. He does not seem to know the aim of the Bill-
Do you know it yourself ?

I am explaining it to the hon. member for ITalton, and if my hon. friend (Mr. Cochrane) wants a special explanation for himself I will give it to him with pleasure. The aim of the Bill is not to take further power to the department, but on the contrary it is to delegate to a commission the powers which the Minister of Marine now has over these harbours. The Bill has been asked for by those specially interested, who believe it would be better to have these harbours administered by those'who live on the spot, rather than by an official who would perhaps take only enough interest in it to get his salary. All the information asked for is contained in the report of the Marine Department; I will send to the library for it and quote it for the benefit of the hon. gentleman.

The Minister of Marine ought to be more familiar with his report than we are, and if it gives him too much trouble to look it up, he can get his officials to do it for him. I think it is a very-I was going to say insolent thing for a minister to tell me, when I ask for information, that I can get it from a report. I am afraid the

minister is losing his head. I want to tell him that he is a servant of the people, controlling an important department, and I don't want him to tell me, when I ask for information, that I can look it up in a report. We pay him for getting that information, and if he is not competent to get it, he had better get out and give some one else the job.
Would you take it ?

No, Sir ; I would not take it. I am not so anxious for a department as some hon. gentlemen, and they had better wait until they get their ambition fulfilled before they ask me whether I would take it. They are waiting, waiting,
[DOT] waiting, for something to turn up, until they can get a job themselves. It is not so funny as they think it is to ask me if 1 would take it, when they know down deep in their hearts that they are waiting for a job, and that just as soon as they get it, they will let somebody else take their place in the House. I wrant to tell the hon. gentleman that he knows, what all the world knows, that the Minister of Public Works was stripped of some of his patronage to gratify the ambition of the Minister of Marine and Fisheries ; and why does he want so much, when he cannot attend to what he has already ? I am here to give an impartial decision on these questions, and this is the way I look at this matter. The minister was very anxious to have more patronage, and he told his constituents that he was going to have it, and the government put themselves in a position to transfer to him a part of the patronage of the Minister of Public Works ; and now when he has got it, he is going to farm it out to a commission. How much are these commissioners going to have ? We pay the Minister of Marine and Fisheries to do the work, and then he says it will be better done by a commission than by one of his officials, who would only do enough to get his salary. I want to know if the hon. minister is sincere in that when he tells me as one of this committee that all his officials think of is to draw their salaries ? We are coming to have government by commission. No matter what little job they have, they transfer it to a commission. I know, Mr. Chairman, that you will sympathize with me in this matter. You are anxious that the money of the electors of your riding should not be frittered away on commissions. The minister is very anxious to talk about his department. If it is his department, he has officials who can hunt up the information when I ask a question ; and if he has not, we will get him another private secretary.

Perhaps I can give the hon. gentleman the information which he asks from the minister. If he looks up the report, he will find that nothing was collected for harbour dues at Fort William or Port
Arthur. The minister states that the fees will not be in excess of those already charged, and the only object of the Bill is to levy harbour dues at Fort William and Port Arthur. This is rather a serious matter. The Canadian Pacific Railway steamers going to Port Arthur are some of them 5,000 tons burden. Under this Bill the fees paid by one of these steamers might be $50 each time it entered the port. They have never been in the habit of paying anything before. Yet, if the promise of the minister is carried out, the Bill will not make any difference, because he says the fees will not be any larger than they are already.

I think the hon. member for South Lanark (Mr. Haggart) is wrong in saying that no fees have been charged ; but he is quite right in this, that there have been no fees returned. I find on page P-137 of the Auditor General's Report that in the province of Ontario there are only two harbours, Fort William and Midland, and that from neither of these have any fees been returned by the officers in charge. I suppose that at each port the harbour master keeps all he can get. I know that American vessel owners have complained that when they come into the harbour of Midland twice during the season they are charged with certain fees, which are generally regulated by the tonnage, while if a Canadian vessel goes to an American port she is not held up in this manner at all. Surely it cannot be that there are only two harbours in the province of Ontario where fees are collected ; or is it that the harbour masters everywhere collect them and put the money into their pockets ? I think in the interest of the country no fees should be levied at all, particularly as there are no fees on the American side. Are the harbour masters of Fort William and Port Arthur to have carte blanche to keep all they can collect, or are they to have as a salary what they do collect ?

I have waited with some expectation of hearing a declaration of policy from the government on what is, tq my mind, a very important question. The tendency of the times is to increase as much as possible the facilities for cheap transportation. No dues can be imposed, as harbour dues or any other kind, that do not after all come out of the pockets of the producers and shippers. This is, to my mind, a question that should rest on better ground than the mere representation of a board of trade, no matter how respectable or influential that body may be. It is a question on which the government should have some policy. I have not yet heard it explained what is to be accomplished by having harbour commissioners, even at small salaries, to catch vessels trading in and out of Canadian ports and to compel them to pay dues. I am astonished that in those days when we have the shipping interests constantly coming to

the government asking that canal dues and other charges be taken off, we should be now making provision for the imposition of a tax which, though small, will always be a load upon the trade, and consequently be a step in a retrograde direction. I should like to have the policy which is involved in this explained. While the sums to be paid to the harbour commissioners are not so large as to alarm anybody, still the expenditure will be useless unless there is some better purpose behind it than appears on the surface.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I have a very distinct recollection that this legislation was passed, as stated by my hon. colleague, at the solicitation of the commercial authorities of these two towns, Port Arthur and Fort William. I have a distinct recollection that the boards of trade asked to be entrusted with the management of these two harbours. These harbours are of recent creation. They are contemporaneous with the establishment of the Canadian Pacific Railway and have been managed up to the present from the city of Ottawa by the Department of Marine and Fisheries. It will not surprise anybody that the citizens and merchants of these two towns should desire to have the management of their own harbours.
Did they put any money into them ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No, nor do they expect to derive any personal profit, but they desire to attract all the trade they can and are engaged in rivalry with all the other harbours. Everywhere on the lakes there is rivalry between harbour and harbour to attract trade, which is very natural aud laudable. The people of these two rising towns pretend that they are better adapted to look after the interests of their own harbours than anybody else, and in that I agree with them. They can do better for themselves and the more business they can attract to their harbours, the more the whole country will profit. Therefore, when they ask to be entrusted with the management of their own harbours, that seems to the government a very natural and reasonable request and a very laudable ambition. There is one thing in which I agree with my hon. friend, and that is that he should not load down the trade of the country with undue taxation, but that all the charges should be kept as low as possible. This Bill does not violate that principle. Each harbour is to be managed by three commissioners to be appointed by the government, and these commissioners give their services gratuitously.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
No, that is what a harbour master gets, and surely that is cheap enough. Under the circum-Mr. CLANCY.
stances the tolls ought to be very low, and I think that the spirit of this measure should call for the commendation and not the criticism of my hon. friend.
Mr. CLANCY". Nobody will object to the spirit of friendly rivalry between these towns and to their desire to manage their own affairs,, but the question to me is whether this Bill provides the best means of increasing and encouraging trade. The power is given here of charging a maximum sum, and to that extent the government loses control entirely.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: No.
They may charge up to one cent per ton but cannot charge more. Up to one cent a ton they can make a charge independently of the government.
No, they must have the approval of the Governor in Council.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: And the Governor in Council cannot approve of a rate exceeding one cent.

That means really a charge of some kind. Though the rate may be nominal, it is charged to a vessel every time it enters the port, no matter how often, and the right hon. gentleman knows that there is always a very natural tendency to increase the revenue, especially when there is means provided for spending it. It would be better to pay out any reasonable sum without getting any return in the way of fees than to impose any fees which would have the slightest tendency to load up the trade.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I agree with you .
I question whether it is wise to create these new powers, which seems to me unnecessary and which it will be difficult for the government to restrain.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
There is a rivalry to-day among the different harbours around the lakes to attract trade. But in the case of Port Arthur and Fort William there is a growing rivalry to make our own end of Lake Superior the rival of Duluth. It is the ambition of Port Arthur aud Fort William to rival that great American port, and it is because of that ambition that they desire to be entrusted with the management of their own harbours. And I think we may trust to their own sense of self-interest not to impose any tax which would deter shipping from coming into their harbours. In their own self interest, they will endeavour to manage their business affairs so economically as to attract business. I am aware, however, of what my hon. friend has in his own mind and I agree with him. The trade is so sensitive that even a small fraction of a cent will effect something of

a diversion from one port to another. And therefore, not only has the government limited. but parliament here will limit, the power to a charge of one cent a ton. But, in case that even a charge of one cent a ton may be excessive, the Governor in Council has supervision of the rate, which must be prepared by the local authorities and submitted to the Governor in Council. We must assume that the harbour board will seek to bring trade to, rather than remove trade from, the harbour.

The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Prefontaine) and the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) have stated that the reason that we have this legislation is that the people of Port Arthur and Fort William desire to control the affairs of their own harbour. How is it that we have exceptional legislation for these two ports V In other ports of the country as Toronto, Montreal, Quebec, all of them great ports- as Port Arthur and Fort William are destined to be great ports-the commissioners are appointed partly by the city council and partly by the Board of Trade. The position of Port Arthur will be much more important in the future than it is at present. The people have expressed a desire to have control of their own port. But, under this Bill every act of the commissioners is subject to the approval of the Governor in *Council. They have no power to even appoint the harbour master, but, under section 8, the harbour master is to be appointed by approval of the Governor in Council. So, the people there are not going to have control of their harbour in the way they must have had in their own minds when they sought this power. What is the length of term for which the commissioners are appointed ?

During good behaviour, just the same as everywhere else.
ilr. KEMP. Then, may I ask the minister what precedent there is for this legislation ? What other harbours of this country have a special Act of this kind ?
Many others-St. John, Halifax, North Sydney, Three Rivers- quite a number of them.
But Quebec, Montreal and Toronto have not ?

Quebec and Montreal have.

It seems to me that, as a test of the good faith with which these powers are asked for for the collection of fees, it should be provided that all fees collected shall be turned over to the Receiver 1
General and become part of the consolidated revenue of Canada. I am very well persuaded that under such conditions, the commissioners would not insist for a moment that any fees should be charged. I wish to repeat that these ports will probably become the most important in Canada. I would urge the Prime Minister to remember that this is the gateway between the east and the west; it is the way by which all the grain must go, at least during a certain period of the year and that grain must be carried by vessel. Any fees must rest as a burden upon that trade, a share of which will have to be borne by those who grow the grain, while those who carry it will pay tile rest. This is unduly taxing commerce. In the very nature of things, these ports being the gateway between the west and the east, the right to charge fees affords opportunities for practically unrestrained means of collecting and expending the public money that should be under the control of parliament and the government. I think a great mistake has been made in the past. Probably some gentlemen of more experience than I have had will not agree with me. But it seems to me that it has been a mistake to permit the harbour commissioners to collect dues and spend the money themselves. There is no reason why money collected in that way should be treated differently from public money received for customs duties, canal tolls or in any other way. I do not say that these moneys have been misused in the past, but I say that the system is not a healthy one, and that these matters should be under control of the government and of parliament. I think the government should be held responsible for every dollar of revenue collected, through whatever channel it may come, and parliament should have something to say in the expenditure of that money. And, though it may seem late in the day, I appeal to the Prime Minister that it is not too late in this growing country of ours, to consider seriously whether all this might not be changed with a viSw to the better management of our .great national harbours. We have a national harbour in Montreal, one in Quebec and others elsewhere, but I think that the greatest shipping harbour in Canada will be at the gateway between the west and the east. Let us spend as freely as the finances of the country will permit to meet the needs of these harbours, and let us make them as good as we can. I think we cannot afford any policy of cheese-paring in matters of that kind, for our national harbours are far too important. I now reiterate what I have just suggested, that the system it is here proposed to continue is an incentive, if you please, iu the hands of the harbour commissioners, where they spend the money themselves to expenditures which might be better made if more completely controlled. I am not ascribing any motives except the

38S8
best. But this is a question of adopting the best system, and I repeat that if fees are to be charged they should be turned over to the Receiver General and become part of the consolidated revenue of Canada. And I repeat also that, if this were done, the commissioners themselves would declare for freeing the ports. Is not that fact alone conclusive proof that we should have no embargo, no charge upon the commerce at these ports ? It seems to me that, above all other places in Canada, these ports are the place where these principles apply. I hope the right lion, gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) will seriously consider the idea of making these absolutely free ports. If we must contribute to the improvement of these harbours, let us do it without hesitation. But to hand over to any other authority power to impose dues upon the commerce at the very gateway between the east and the west is I think a very great mistake.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I must say to my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy) with perfect candour, that I am not prepared to take issue with him in the suggestion he has offered not only with reference to this harbour but to all those harbours which may be fairly considered national harbours. But I have only to observe at this moment that what he proposes amounts to an absolute revolution in what has hitherto been the practice in Canada-not only in Canada, but I think in most civilized nations of the earth. Not only in Canada but everywhere, so far as my information goes, I think all harbour dues collected in a harbour are spent by the authorities of that harbour, and for the harbour itself. It is so in Montreal to-day, it is so in Quebec, and I believe it is so in all the large harbours of the Dominion. I do not say that the hon. gentleman is wrong, far from it; I believe there is a good deal to be said in favour of his suggestion. I believe there is indeed a great deal to be said in favour of the proposition that we should make the harbours absolutely free. On the other hand, this would involve a very heavy charge upon the exchequer, and is a thing which, while laudable in itself, requires a good deal of consideration before we adopted it. I do not think however that in a Bill of this kind we should assume to deal with this harbour in a different manner from that which the government has followed with regard to every other harbour. Therefore whilst there is a good deal to be said in favour of the position of my hon. friend, all I can say at this moment is that the Bill ought to be allowed to go through its regular course before we undertake to consider the proposition of my hon. friend. But as he has made the proposition, it involves a very serious revolution in our policy. In respect to the harbour of Montreal, we shall have to consider at no distant day whether we ought not to make it absolutely duty free. If we do that in Mr. CLANCY.
Montreal, we will have to do it in Halifax, we will have to do it in St. John, and perhaps also with the harbours on the lakes. Before we adopt such a revolutionary policy we should take ample time to consider it.

I understand it is the intention of the government to collect dues at each of these ports. Would the premier for instance collect those dues from one vessel or boat at each of the ports of Port Arthur and Fort William ? I am almost inclined to think he would. Again I would ask how far down the lake from Port Arthur would these commissioners have jurisdiction, besides having control of the harbour itself-how many miles ? It strikes me that this Bill would give the commissioners absolute jurisdiction a long way down the lake.

At the present time these harbours do not exist as regularly organized harbours. By this Bill it is proposed that a commission shall take charge of the harbour of Port Arthur and organize it as a harbour, or as a port. Now it stands to reason that certain expenses will be connected with this organization, and it is provided in the Bill that such rates or dues as may be imposed will all be controlled by the government, just as if the government were to take hold of it at the present time and appoint officers there to look after the port. Therefore I do not see that it makes much difference whether this port is administered by the department here through officers appointed by the department, or whether it is administered by a commission of gentlemen chosen in the town and having a stake in the locality. It is provided further down in this Bill that all moneys which may be collected there will go first to pay the salaries of the harbour master, because the commissioners receive no pay ; and the balance of whatever money is collected will be used for lighting, buoying and similar purposes, in order to equip the harbour properly. As I have already said, that can be done in two ways-by a harbour commission consisting of local gentlemen, or by the department at Ottawa. But the people there have requested us to organize the port with a board of commissioners, who will see that the necessary improvements are made, and provide for whatever needs to be done in the harbour. Now the rates that it is proposed to impose will all be controlled by the government, there can be no difficulty about that. The same rule will be applied to this harbour as is applied to the harbours in Montreal, in Quebec, in Halifax, and every other city where there is a harbour commission. As I have already had occasion to state, the tendency is to decrease the cost of the administration of these harbours, and to make as little charge as possible upon the trade, or on the ships that frequent these ports.

The question raised by the hon. member lor Bothwell (Mr. Clancy) is a very important one, but it would involve this government in assuming debts or liabilities to the amount of many millions of dollars. It is to be remembered that at this moment the harbour commissioners of Montreal are indebted in the sum of $10,000,000, the interest on which is provided for by dues charged in the harbour. These rates have not been increased, on the contrary they have been reduced during the last few years. The commissioners are about tc enter upon another expenditure to the extent of $3,000,000. which will [DOT] make the debt of the harbour commission of Montreal amount to $13,000,000. I do not exactlj know what is the debt of the harbour commission of Quebec. But if the government were to adopt the policy of assuming the liabilities of the various harbours, I am quite sure they would amount to not less than from $15,000,000 to $20,000,000. Well, the time may come when such a liability will be assumed by this country, but I do not think we are in a position to assume that liability at present, particularly in connection with this Bill.

The policy of assuming the harbour debt would not be different from that of granting bounties to various industries. With regard to accounting for the fees for shipping as intended in this Bill, would that include an auditor to act for the government ? Now the minister did not answer my question. I asked how far down the lake would this Bill give the commissioners jurisdiction, how far from Port Arthur ? The reason I ask is this : The harbour commissioners of Montreal are residents of that city and no doubt the harbour commissioners of Port Arthur would be residents of that town, and they will be more concerned about the interests of Port Arthur than about any other portion of the shores of the lake for many miles. The same may be said with regard to Fort William. With regard to the tolls, I would ask the minister whether it would not be a good thing if the port of Montreal were made free.

It would certainly be a good thing if the port of Montreal was free and the trade of the country would be very well satisfied if that could be brought about. Of course if the principle was applied to Montreal it would have to be applied generally and the country would have to assume a very large liability. I am not very familiar with the distances but the description of the harbour is given in section 2 and as far as I can make out, the harbour would comprise from 10 to 15 miles.

It is not so much a question of administration as one of policy that is involved in what has been suggested by /the hon. member for Bothwell (Mr. Clancy). No one, I am sure, doubts that 123
the commissioners to be selected from the citizens of Port Arthur would administer the affairs of the harbour in the most efficient possible way. It is not a criticism upon that phase of the Bill that is being made. The question submitted by my hon. friend is whether the government" shall or shall not use its utmost efforts, and adopt every possible safeguard to prevent any handicapping of these ports by the imposition of rates which might increase the danger of competition from the south. It seems to me that all of the ports in the east are very much interested in the welfare of Port Arthur and Fort William. I say that for this reason that the bringing of traffic to those two ports and the shipping of the grain from those ports is in the highest possible degree essential to the welfare of ports like Montreal and the maritime provinces. If you bring traffic to Port Arthur and ship it along Canadian routes, the eastern ports, on the St. Lawrence and on the Atlantic seaboard, Will obviously if proper safeguards are adopted have a better chance of traffic than if the grain goes to Duluth. The government must bear in mind that there is very fierce competition to the south of us, and that the bringing of eastern bound traffic to those ports is only a partial step towards keeping it in Canadian territory and shipping it from Canadian seaports. For that reason, it seems to me it would be unwise, except in case of the utmost possible necessity, for the government to impose any restrictions, by the exacting of rates or otherwise, which would in any way militate against the future of those ports. The people of Fort William and Port Arthur themselves are of course obviously interested in the freedom of the ports from the imposition of rates which would tend to divert traffic to the south. I am not sufficiently informed to know just what the conditions as to shipments from Duluth are. I have sent out, for some information which I shall have here in a moment, showing the relative distance of Port Arthur and Fort William from central shipping points in the west as compared with the distance of those points from Duluth by a railway which might, and probably will, be built. Having before us the possible danger -of diversion of traffic by direct communication between the great shipping points of the west and Duluth, ought we not, before entering upon a policy of this kind, to pause and consider what the conditions as to shipment at Duluth are and to consider especially whether or not a measure of this kind might not put us out of the race eventually and perhaps in the near future ? We have a great competing port in Duluth, which as I understand is marvellously well equipped, and where the conditions are not of a character to deter in any way traffic from passing to that point.



Has the Minister of Marine any information to give to the House as to the conditions 'of shipment at Duluth. It seems to me that is one of the very first things to consider in debating this Bill. We are authorizing here a rate up to a certain point which of course must be approved by the Governor in Council. It is all very well to have that safeguard ; I am not dealing so much with that as with the policy of the government as here set out which points to the exaction of a tonnage rate on every ship entering these two harbours. I understand the distance from Winnipeg to Fort William and Port Arthur by the Canadian Pacific Railway is about 426 miles, by the Canadian Northern, that distance is about 438 miles, and I also understand that it is quite possible to build a line from Winnipeg to Duluth which will not exceed 384 miles, between 370 and 384 miles. There is another line I believe almost immediately available which would not exceed 431 miles. Therefore the contention is that taking Winnipeg as a central shipping point you have a possible line to Duluth 60 or 70 miles shorter than the line from Winnipeg to these two ports. Thus you are face to face with a possibly very aggressive competition and you are now face to face with a competition by a line of I believe 431 miles in length. That line is either available now or can be made available almost immediately. Another line which would be much shorter, from 370 to 384 miles, could be built I suppose this year. In view of this it seems to me the Minister of Marine should have considered very carefully the- conditions of shipment at Duluth before embarking on a policy of imposing rates on tonnage entering these ports. Let me not be understood as saying that there should be for a moment any retarding of development of those ports ; I believe they should be developed and should be equipped, but I do not think they should be developed and equipped in such a way as to handicap them in the fierce competition which no doubt will exist, if it does not now exist between those ports and the port of Duluth.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The difference in the length of the lines being only about 50 miles, 42 miles, because the distance from Winnipeg to Port Arthur is 426 miles and the distance from Winnipeg to Duluth 384 miles. A distance of 42 miles does not count very seriously after all. The rate between Winnipeg and the harbours on Lake Superior over all lines will necessarily be the rate over the shortest and therefore the cheapest line. ' All others will have to meet the rate of that line. The suggestion made by my hon. friend (Mr. R. L. Borden) and by the hon. member for Both well (Mr. Clancy) that we should not unduly burden the harbours on the lakes and perhaps should not burden them at all, Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
but should make them absolutely free ports is a proposition which is deserving of serious consideration.
I must say that when this Bill was prepared, we simply acted upon the petition of the merchants of Fort William and Port Arthur, and did not take that matter into consideration. If we adopt the policy of making these harbours free ports, we must apply that policy generally, and we cannot do that except upon a very comprehensive plan. We all agree that these harbours must be developed, and we thought we could npt do better than to develop them on the plan suggested by the commercial interests of these young and rising ports. There is not to-day a harbour in the Dominion which has not been developed along the same system of local authorities authorized by parliament to levy tolls with which to improve the harbours. The idea suggested by my hon. friend is not new ; it is now engaging the attention of the Transportation Commission, and in the meantime we thought we could not do better than to develop this harbour on the lines hitherto pursued.
The policy of the government during the past few years had been to remove as far as possible all charges upon transportation, and that policy has been partially carried out.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That has been our policy, and its object is to help the St. Lawrence route.

I am not proposing to discuss the general policy at present for I have already expressed my opinion with regard to it. However, that policy does not stand in our way if we carry out the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. Clancy). We do not want to put Port Arthur and Fort William into such a position that in the future we may have to undo our work with respect to them as well as with respect to all our national ports. No injustice is done to eastern Canadian ports by making Port Arthur and Fort William free, because the ports of Montreal, Quebec, St. John and Halifax are in a very great measure interested in having these inland ports free, inasmuch as the better chance you give to these ports to compete with Duluth, the better chance our eastern Canadian ports have to. get the trade. The government should very* carefully consider the advisability of embarking on a policy such as is set forth in this Bill. I say this in the interests of not only Port Arthur and Fort William, but also in the interests of our grain trade, of the farmers of the west, and of our national ports on the St. Lawrence and in the maritime provinces ? I think that the government should delay pressing this Bill through, in order to see first whether the public interests generally do not demand

that these ports should be made absolutely free and national inland ports in the true sense of the term.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is a good deal in the suggestion of my hon. friend (Mr. It. L. Borden) and I would advise my hon. friend the Minister of Marine to go through the clauses of the Bill, but not to take it out of committee.
I would suggest that the government should await the report of their Transportation Commission, so that they may have information to enable them to intelligently deal with this question.

I will not press the Bill to a third reading until the matter is further considered. When I adopted the idea of the persons locally interested in preparing this Bill, the larger question involved did not present itself to my mind. I have visited Duluth in the capacity of harbour commissioner of Montreal, and as far as I can remember, although I do not speak with confidence, Duluth is not a public port, but is controlled by large private companies.

The harbour dues in Montreal and Quebec are collected for the use of the docks, and in the case of Montreal, probably also for deepening the channel. There is no parallel between these harbour dues and the tax proposed by this Bill. The docks now exist in Port Arthur and belong to the great railways, .and if other docks are built those who build them will have the right to charge for their use. If we should pass this Bill we would be establishing the principle of a government tax upon transportation.
Not having before us information with regard to the taxes imposed at Duluth and other American ports. I think it would be a mistake to adopt that principle with refer-erence to Port Arthur and Fort William, which are the only Canadian ports on the great lakes which are likely to be of great importance. While the tax is small, it would constantly stare shippers in the face, and might be the means of diverting trade to American ports. Therefore, whatever is done with this Bill ultimately, I hope that the government will in the future as they have done in the past, assume the small liability which this tax represents. I would like to ask whether it was understood by the parties who petitioned for this legislation that the government would appoint all the commissioners. It is customary, as the minister knows, for the city council and the Board of Trade to participate with the government in the appointment of harbour commissioners, and it seems to me that it would be advisable to give the citizens of Port Arthur and' Fort William an opportunity of appointing one or perhaps two of these commissioners.

That is why I asked the minister about the appointment of the commissioners-whether the people of Port Arthur and Fort William signified to him either verbally or in writing that they would like to elect one or more of the commissioners themselves ?
No, the question was never raised.

I do not want to oppose the passage of clause 7, but I do feel that if

3S96
you once admit the principle of this harbour tax, which is different altogether from harbour dues, you will he committing a grave mistake under all the circumstances.

To my mind this is a much more far reaching question than it appeared to he when the Bill was introduced or even when it was read this afternoon. I am glad this discussion has taken place, because it has brought more forcibly to our minds the great importance of the two ports, Fort William and Port Arthur. The. minister has told us that he was moved to introduce these two Bills by a petition from these two towns. Now, it occurs to me that there are a great many people just as much interested in these ports as are the people living in Fort William and Port Arthur. To my mind not only should they have been consulted, but the people of Winnipeg should have been consulted, and also the people of Regina, Calgary and all the other towns in that western country, because practically these are their ports. These ax-e the ports through which the transportation from the west to the east to a very large extent must pass ; and to my mind it is not fair to give the towns of Port Arthur and Fort William power to impose a tax on the immense traffic that will originate in the western country and pass through those ports to the eastern parts of the Dominion and on to the ocean. It seems to me that the minister should have gone much further than simply to .Port Arthur and Fort William for authority to introduce these Bills. It seems to me that all the people of the west should have been consulted. At any rate, their interest should have been consulted, because they are the people who are to pay the tax which is to be imposed upon transportation passing through these ports. I think the minister would do well to pause even till another session before committing himself to the policy which is suggested in these two Bills, and carefully consider the question as to whether or not the government could wisely make these two ports exceptional cases in the great transportation problem of this country.
To my mind they are exceptional cases, and ought to be dealt with in an exceptional way. We are abandoning in a great deal of our legislation all former precedents and laying down new rules in the best interests of the country ; and, in my opinion, -the fact that a certain policy was adopted in bygone years of placing certain harbours under the authority of a commission ought not to prevent us from changing our methods, if the new ways are better than the old ones. I regard the harbours of Fort William and Port Arthur, more especially Fort William, as two of the most important In this country. I know of none in the Dominion equal to the harbour of Fort William. That can be made an excellent commodious harbour at very much less cost than any we know of in this country. Along the banks of the Mr. KEMP.	_
Ivaministiquia jjou can have twenty-five miles of docks, including the Mission river, at practically very small cost to the country, because these docks are being constructed by private enterprise. The dredging of the river, *which would be the chief item of expense, would not be very expensive. Looking at these two harbours from every standpoint, they are of an exceptional nature. Their location midway between the east and the west, on the route over which the greater part of the traffic of the great west will pass to the east, warrants us in treating them in a very exceptional manner. So far as I am concerned, I am quite prepared to say that these ports should be made free, and that we should not tax the people of the great west for the privilege of transporting their goods through them. What we are trying to do is to remove burdens and not to impose them. We are discussing the question of giving increased facilities for the carriage of the traffic of that great western country, and why should we spend large sums to cheapen transportation and then place in the hands of three men in Port Arthur and three in Fort William power to impose taxes on transportation from west to east ? The hon. minister will do well to give this matter further consideration. He ought, in all fairness, to consult the people west of Port Arthur and Fort William, who are interested even to a greater extent than the citizens of these two towns. I hope that the minister will not hurry the matter through, but give it his most mature consideration. It will be well for us to start right. These are simply new ports, not yet organized, and in a different position from Montreal, Halifax or Quebec. Whatever changes we are going to make in our system of dealing with the harbours of this country, here is a grand opportunity for the Minister of Marine to exercise his judgment, and not start out in a way that he may regret five or ten years hence and which may compel him, or whoever may then be in his position, to change the system and adopt a new one. The imposing of this tax by the people of Port Arthur and Fort William on the traffic of the country is going to be an additional burden on the west, and he should hesitate before taking a step in that direction. These two ports are twin ports, and it is quite possible that a vessel may have to go to Port Arthur and, after loading partially there, finish her cargo at Fort William. Would it be fair to impose two taxes on that vessel one after another ? I am glad to know that the hon. minister will not press this Bill to a final reading to-night, but will give us another opportunity of discussing the question. After visiting the city of Montreal last year and viewing the harbour, I was very deeply impressed with the improvements being made there, and on my return from Montreal I expressed the opinion, which I stand by to-day, that I regretted very much Montreal

hacl not been made a free port. I hope that at no%ar distant day it will.

I do not think that the committee can say that the mover of this Bill has not proceeded with a great deal of deliberation. It was introduced last year simply as a notice to all interested and not carried, and I understand has been submitted to and approved by the authorities of Fort William and Port Arthur. It seems to me that the Bill is in the right direction. Both those harbours are becoming great and important, and it is necessary that they should be placed under proper jurisdiction. The fact that a small fee is to be levied is only in accordance with the practice followed in other harbours of the Dominion ; and until we decide to make the great harbours free, I do not see how we could proceed to make Port Arthur and Fort William free. The great object of the government has been to try and divert the grain traffic through Canadian channels. We all know and regret the fact that 230,000,000 to 240,000,000 bushels of grain go to the port of Buffalo every year, counting wheat, meal and flour as grain, while a comparatively insignia. cant quantity goes down to Montreal and Quebec, and the government are trying to change this condition. They have removed the tolls from the Welland and St. Lawrence canals, and by that means have removed one of the barriers which obstructed trade to Montreal and Quebec. They have also carried through with considerable success the improvements of these great ports, and it is not to our credit as a country that until the last three or four years nothing was done in the great harbour of Montreal at all.
The facilities for handling grain there were fifty years behind the times. Vessels unloading there could make only 4,000 bushels an hour while, in the great city of Buffalo they would unload grain at the rate of
50,000	or 60,000 bushels an hour. It is no wonder that trade did not seek outlet at Montreal. The government have wisely in my opinion, attempted to remove the difficulties in the way. In the first place they have removed the tolls on the canals. That has had a beneficial effect, for a much larger (Quantity of grain has gone down our highway this year than went down before. The government have also spent large sums in improving the terminal facilities at Montreal, which will be another attraction to the Canadian route. Now, it seems to me that, if you are to go further, if you are to attempt to make any harbours free, it would be better to begin with one of the harbours below the Welland canal. You are aw'are, Mr. Chairman, that a large quantity of the grain that comes through Port Arthur goes to Buffalo. To make those ports free would not divert the grain to the Canadian route. But, if you started at the other end and begin your experiment
by making one of the eastern ports free, the effect would be beneficial to our own transportation system. The time will come, probably, when all these harbours will be made free. But that time has not yet arrived. I do not think the Dominion of Canada is prepared, at the present time, to assume the burden of all these great harbours. It would be an enormous undertaking. We have spent $G0,000.000 in the canals and the working of these costs a very large sum every year, for which there is no return as the canals are free. If we are to assume the harbour at Quebec, the harbour at Montreal, the harbour at Halifax, St. John, Fort William, Port Arthur, Hamilton and all the other important harbours on the Great Lakes, it wTonld be a tremendous undertaking and one that we should not enter upon now'.
Can the hon. minister tell me the tonnage entering and leaving Port Arthur and Fort William last year ?
I have not that information.

I am not very familiar with how this proposed tonnage scheme will work out, but I think it is more serious than the bon. minister believes it to be. Take a vessel of 2,000 tons plying between Port Arthur or Fort William and one of our ports on Georgian bay. In the season it would make probably twenty-eight trips. That would be a tax on that vessel during the season of $560. That is an enormous tax. And, if the vessel has to call at both ports, as many of them have to do, the tax would be doubled. In the future, the system of calling at both ports will probably be more general. I understand that very large terminal elevators are being erected at Port Arthur, and the cleaning elevators will be there. Supposing a vessel of 2,000 tons left Fort William and called at Port Arthur to complete her cargo, the dues in the course of a season would amount to over $1,100. A vessel of 2,000 tons is not very large even now, and probably they will increase rapidly in size. I believe that in the next five years many of our vessels will be 3,000 tons. The charge on such a vessel would be $740, or, if calling at both ports, $1,480. That is a line that would tell very heavily against Port Arthur and Fort William, and I think the tendency would be to send the traffic to Duluth. If my figures are right, and, of course, I have had no opportunity to verify them, this proposal is, as I say, a more serious one, I believe, than the minister supposes it to be. I am sure that the proposed fees of 1 cent a ton is out of all proportion. I do not think there is any such tax levied on any port in this country.

My hon. friend from West York (Mr. Campbell) seemed to be under the impression that there was a desire on this side of the House to oppose legislation
3S99

'for the benefit of these two very important ports. But that is not the direction that this discussion has taken so far as this side is concerned.
Only as to the question whether they should be free. I understood the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) to contend that they should be free.

If inconsistency was not a chief feature in the character of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell) and of the government he supports, I should be inclined to express my surprise at his using as an argument in favour of the principle involved in this Bill, the circumstance that the government has taken the tolls off the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. I think if he had stopped for a moment to consider that fact he would not have referred to it. The fact is, as every member of this House knows, that the government did, in its wisdom, see fit to take the tolls off the Welland and St. Lawrence canals. Let me ask for what purpose they did that. For the purpose, as expressed at the time,, of increasing the traffic by those canals, and to give shippers the benefit of cheaper means of transportation. Almost immediately after they had performed that act-and I may say it is not so old that it has escaped the memory of the hon. member for West York (Mr. Campbell)-

Didn't I say so ?
Mr, PORTER. This government saw lit to pass through this House a measure for the construction of what they are pleased to call a transcontinental railway, 400 miles north to take the traffic away from these canals that they were professing to help. The principle involved in this Bill is not a new principle. There are many harbours in the Dominion of Canada that are today being operated under commissions appointed by this or former governments. I have had some personal experience with the management of a particular harbour under a commission appointed by this government. I am not disposed to quarrel with the principle involved in this mil and am not in a position to say whether the administration of the more important harbours of this country would be better under commissions than under the local authorities, but I am bound to say from my experience that I am led to the conclusion that the administration of these harbours by the local authorities is better than their administration under a commission. I am led to that conclusion from one particular case. In that case a petition was presented to the government by the board of trade just as a petition has been presented in the case dealt with by this Bill and it was conceived by the board of trade and by the municipal council at

tliat time, that it would be to the advantage of the municipality that that harbour should be administered by a commission rather than by the municipality itself. That petition found favour in the eyes of the government then in power and a commission was appointed ; the harbour was taken out of the control of the municipality and I think every respectable man in the municipality of which I am speaking, will endorse the statement that the government of that time not this government appointed to that position three men as responsible, as respectable, and as interested as could possibly have been appointed under the circumstances. The mayor of the city was one, the chairman of the executive committee of the council was another and a gentleman who had been engaged in mercantile pursuits in the city I am referring to, was the third, a gentleman who had had experience upon the council for many years and who was perfectly familiar wTith all the details of the harbour. During the two or three years of that commission's administration the harbour prospered. and was very greatly improved and the people generally who were shipping by and through that port were pleased with the result. But unfortunately there came a change of government and here is where I have a suspicion, a very strong suspicion that the Bill now introduced is introduced for the purpose of party advancement rather than for the advancement of the country as
whole. Notwithstanding that commission was then appointed and was operating the harbour to the great improvement of the trade of the harbour and to the general satisfaction of the public, a change in the harbour board came with the change of government and instead of three such gentlemen as I have already mentioned having control of the harbour of the city to which I am now referring, the government saw tit to appoint one man who resided no less than 14 or 15 miles from the harbour to which I am referring as one of these harbour commissioners.
An lion. MEMBER. What harbour ?

1 think the Hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries understands perfectly well to what harbour 1 refer. A gentleman was appointed who resided 14 or 15 miles from the harbour. He knew no more about the harbour of that place than a goose knows about its grandmother. He saw fit to hold on and the government saw fit to allow him to hold on as harbour commissioner, until the local election in Ontario occurred and then this harbour commissioner resigned his position and ran for the local legislature. He was defeated and the province of Ontario or the riding in which he ran is to be congratulated on that defeat, but as soon as he was defeated he was reappointed to the position and he to-day occupies the position of harbour commissioner although he knows no more about the harbour of Mr. PORTER.
which he is a commissioner than I know about British Columbia. That state of affairs existed for some time until a second election was called and then this gentleman again ran and was defeated again, and still he is harbour commissioner of the harbour to which I refer. That is not the orly example:	instead of the gentleman
to whom I have referred, who had been engaged in business in the city adjoining the harbour for 30 odd years and who enjoyed the confidence of every business man and every respectable person in the municipality, a man who was perfectly familiar with all the details of the harbour being allowed to continue in office, the government appointed the editor of the ' Ontario ' newspaper which supports this government, who knows no more about harbours or the administration of harbour affairs than, as I said before, a goose knows about its grandmother. Thus, the harbours to which I refer has been carried on, and it is for this reason that I believe that the administration of the harbours of this country by a commission, if this government is going to follow the precedent that it has already laid down by appointing partisans, by appointing political hacks, by appointing people who know nothing about the condition of a harbour or how it should be administered, is not in the interests of the municipalities concerned, or in the interests of the country as a w'hole. The board of trade in that ease petitioned the government of the day to appoint this harbour,commission. But to-day if a vote was taken of the board of trade every man of them -would hold up his hand to say:	Revoke the charter
you have given to the harbour commissioners and let us have it under the old regime. They are feeling to-day the evil effects of the administration of the harbour under commissioners of whom I spoke. I had occasion, not more than two years ago, to call the attention of the hon. Minister of Marine and Fisheries and the hon. Minister of Customs to a grievance that exists at the port to which I referred. A very large canning factory is carried on in this municipality and fruits as well as corn, tomatoes, peas, and other products of the farm that are grown within a radius of 25 miles of this canning factory are shipped in the adjoining county not more than a mile or a mile and a half from this port by little boats plying -Up and down the Bay of Quinte and these boats are brought into the harbour at Belleville and their cargoes taken to the canning factory. [DOT]
Belleville is the port.

Yes, Belleville is the port,
and I am ashamed to say it is being so treated. Those gentlemen who are running this canning factory are obliged to pay harbour dues to the commissioners on these products, and when they asked for relief the

commissioners refused to grant it. If that port were in the hands of the municipality, the municipality could grant relief, and the municipality would derive much greater *benefit than it derives now. I quite agree ,with the hon. member for Halton, that the hon. Minister of Marine ought to give the greatest consideration to this Bill, because there are large interests involved. Port Arthur and Fort William are the key of the transportation question from the west to the east. They ought not to be dealt with as ordinary ports, but they should be considered in the light of the solution of our transportation problem ; and political interests should not be allowed to interfere with their development.

The ' Huronic ' was built in Coilingwood a couple of years ago, and was perhaps the best vessel built in- Canada up to that date. Her net registered tonnage is 2,216, and she makes a trip at least once a week from Coilingwood to Port Arthur, calling at Owen Sound. Assuming that she makes twenty-eight trips in the season, that, at one cent a ton, would mean $616 in fees at Port Arthur, and if she called at Fort William also it would mean $1,222. If you give the harbour commissioners at Port Arthur and Fort William the right to charge one cent a ton you could not deny the same right to Coilingwood and Owen Sound, and il the ' Huronic ' called at these two latter ports and they charged one cent a ton, it would mean a total tax of $2,464 a season on this one vessel. Such a tax would probably mean the driving of all these vessels out of business altogether. I am quite sure that the shippers have no idea that it is contemplated by the government to give the commissioners at Port Arthur and Fort William the powers set out in this Bill. I hope the minister will let the Bill stand until the shipping interests are consulted.
These harbour commissioners could only exercise the powers provided for in this Bill with the approval of the Governor in Council.
And if the government refused to allow them to charge one cent per ton, it would be natural that they would make a demand upon the government to spend money on their harbour.

Not at all. It does not follow that the government would allow them to impose a tariff which would be detrimental to the port. I admit that the maximum tariff of one cent a ton is high, but I do not suppose that the local authorities would impose any fee that would be detrimental to their ports. I may say that these Bills were introduced last year, and were read a second time and printed, remaining on the order paper until the end of the session. We heard no complaint whatever about them ; but, on the contrary, those interested requested that the government
should endeavour to have them passed into legislation. However, the discussion this afternoon has been very fruitful of information. I have no desire to press the Bill on until an opportunity is given for further consideration. In reply to a question asked by an hon. gentleman, I may say that during the year 1903 the number of vessels arriving at Fort William was 332 ; tonnage, 395,000 tons; number of vessels departed, 303; tonnage, 343,000 ; number of vessels arrived at Port Arthur, 199 ; tonnage, 62,850 ; departures, 204 ; tonnage, 63,600. Comparing that port with the port of Quebec, we find that in Quebec during the last season the arrivals were 543 vessels, with a tonnage of
744.000	tons ; and the departures, 630 vessels, with a tonnage of 1,012,000 tons.

I find that the figures in the Trade and Navigation returns for the fiscal year ending the 30th June, 1903, do not correspond with those given by the minister. They give the number of vessels arriving at Fort William at 430 with a tonnage of
539.000	tons and the departures at 413 with a tonnage of 438,000 tons. At Port Arthur the arrivals were 23S with a tonnage of
246.000	tons and the departures 305 with a tonnage of 396,600 tons. These returns are evidently on their face wrong.

My returns are for the last season to the close of navigation, while the statement read by the hon. gentleman evidently comprises the season from the 1st of July, 1902 to the 1st of July, 1903. I move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Is there any objection to my hon. friend bringing down the correspondence in reference to these two Bills ?
There is no objection.
Perhaps my hon. friend would lay on the table of the House what information he can collect with regard to the system adopted in the port of Duluth.

I will try to procure the information. I may state at once, from the information I have gathered, that the statement that there are free ports in the United States is not exactly true. There are ports where there is no direct charge made, but the charge is made indirectly by being included in the railway charges when the terminals are controlled by railways.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister a question in reference to a document which the ex-Minister of Public Works, the hon. member for St. Mary's (Mr. Tarte), states that he handed to the Prime Minister two years before he resigned his office, bearing on the question of making Montreal a free port. To make clear what I refer to, I will read from the hon. gentleman's statement in ' Hansard ' of May 3, at page 2489 :

With that object in view, a couple of years before I left office, I placed before the Prime Minister a public document-not a private document-in which I suggested, amongst other things, that the Montreal harbour debt should be assumed by the federal government, and that the port of Montreal should be equipped to handle the trade that is in store for it.
Would the Prime Minister have any objection to laying that document on the table of the House in order that we may have it before us in considering this measure ?

I quite agree with the hon. member. nation, and will be able to bring down the report of his engineer or architect on the subject.

That would refer to new work, but this is work which has to be done while the departments are in charge of the building, and it would be difficult to lay out a contract and ask for tenders under the circumstances.

Last year we had a discussion about the analysts. Has any change been made in the custom, or are you continuing the work as it was carried on last year ?

I have not made any change in regard to that matter since I entered the department. There are district analysts to whom samples are sent fon
analysis, and also some samples are sent to the head office here.

But, according to my recollection, prosecutions were impossible because, while the district analyst was the party who. ought to be employed to make the analysis, and who would be available to give evidence, the samples were sent here, and the chain of evidence necessary to conviction of the party was broken. I have not the law before me, but that is my remembrance of the matter. The district analysts did the work for years. But, for some reason unknown to the House, they were dropped. Their names remain there, but they are not given any work to do.

I think my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) is misinformed. I do not think we are bound by the law to send samples to the district analyst. The evidence could be given just as well, and perhaps in a more efficient way, by the analyst at the head office. I think that was not where the trouble came in. The law provided, and if I remember well, that the district analyst should collect the samples

No, the law provides that the samples shall be collected by parties employed for the purpose. In all large centres we have men who do that work. Ri Montreal I know a man is busy collecting these samples for analysis.

I do not intend to deal with the matter to-night, because I have not it sufficiently clear in my memory to give the salient points. But I went over it last year and found that po prosecutions were made under the law. My recollection is that the explanation given to me was that there was a break in the chain of evidence and a case could not be established. At that time I had the law before me, and I remember that it was quite clear to me at that time why you could not prosecute successfully. The fact that prosecutions did not take place is at legist prima facie evidence that there was something wrong. The law was violated, but there were no prosecutions.
Mr. BRODEUR, I know that there was some difficulty in the way I have mentioned-some district analysts instead of analysing the samples, had them analysed by outsiders.
No, that was not the trouble.

Besides, if I remember the law, it is not specially provided that the

analysis should be made by the district analyst. It can be made at the head office. As to prosecutions, I may say that, in most eases where it has been found that food is adulterated, we have thought it as well to impose as penalty the cost of the analysis, which is very heavy. My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) knows more about that than I do, having a knowledge of chemistry. No analysis that we make, I believe, costs less than $15. It seems to me that that could hardly have been the experience. Mr. BRODiEUR. I have not the figures of last year, but the hon. gentleman will see that we are asking the same amount for next year as was voted for this year.
