How many fines were imposed by the department ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REVENUE.
It is not easy to tell that off-hand, because these penalties are exacted by the collectors of the different divisions. I can bring down a statement if my hon. friend wishes.

Then you did not go into the courts at all ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REVENUE.
No.

Why not ?
The	MINISTER	OF	INLAND	REVENUE.
Because we are at liberty to settle	these cases,
provided the party who is found guilty is will-Mr. BRODEUR.
ing to do so. We can either impose a penalty or go into court.

Were any samples except fertilizers and Paris green taken last year ?
The MINISTER OF INLAND jREVENUE. Yes. There were 100 samples of fertilizers and 150 samples of Paris green. WTe had also honey, 100 samples ; flavouring extracts, 100 ; canned meat, 100 ; and canned vegetables, 100. These are now undergoing analysis. We have reports of canned meats and fertilizers, which have been published in the bulletin. The balance remains to be published.
These are all the articles of food or beverages collected during the past year ?
Yes.

As I read the Act, you could not sustain a prosecution at all. The first clause provides howT the samples shall be obtained by the outside analyst. He shall obtain three samples, one of which he shall put up and send to the department, one he shall give to the party handling or selling the goods, and the third he shall retain and examine himself. The prosecution must take place only after the analysis of the outside analyst, not after the analysis of the central analyst ; and if the prosecution is sustained and the party desires to appeal, he appeals to the chief analyst here, and not till then. I venture to say that you could not sustain a prosecution upon an analysis first obtained from the chief analyst. You might patch up a case and fix a penalty, and the individual breaking the law might be willing to pay it without going any further ; but otherwise you could not sustain a prosecution. If the procedure as defined in the Act is not followed out by the department in the regular order, I do not think it could sustain a prosecution. For these reasons I think the Act is violated, and it is practically of little use. It is for the reason, I think,, that we have had no prosecutions lately, and very little has been done in the last few years.
As I pointed out last year, tbe law provides that the samples shall be collected by the outside analyst, and that he shall analyse. Then when a prosecution took place, he would give evidence, and if the party were not satisfied, he appealed to the department here and the chief analyst was practically a court of appeal.
Mi*. BRODEUR. The samples are collected by the food inspector and not by the analyst.
The law provides that they shall be collected by the analyst.

No. Generally the samples are collected by the food inspector and two of the samples taken are sent to Ottawa, one of which is analysed by Mr. McGill, or one of the other assistant analysts, and then an appeal may be made from the assistant analyst to the chief analyst.
You would not prosecute under the analysis of one officer of your department, and then: appeal to another departmental officer?
The law so provides.
As I understand it, the outside analyst makes the analysis and is examined to prove the charge. If the party is dissatisfied he can appeal to the department here.

It is within the discretion of the minister to have the analysis made by one of the departmental analysts, and it is not necessary that it should be made by the district analyst. That is where my hon. friend is mistaken.
The law says that one sample shall be given to the district analyst who shall analyse it.

The minister can decide by whom the analysis shall be made. The law formerly was that the analysis should be made by the district analyst alone, but the law has been amended and now the samples are sent to Ottawa and analysed by one of the assistant analysts. If we are not satisfied, there may be an appeal to the chief analyst.
There were many samples collected, and many were found to be adulterated, but why have there been no prosecutions?

Most of the people were fined. My hon. friend will find, if he becomes Minister of Inland Revenue one of these days, that it is rather hard to prosecute and have large fines imposed upon poor dealers in the country, who sometimes are found selling things which are adulterated without having any knowledge of the fact. The best way is to compel them to pay a penalty in the shape of the'cost of the analysis. I admit that in some cases ([DOT]samples should be made, and I intend to carry out the law as efficiently as possible.
I think it is very important that there should be publicity given to the prosecutions, so that they will serve as a warning to others.
They are published in the bulletins.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: On page K-23 of the Auditor General's Report, I find that the department purchased from W. H. Sproule, Ottawa, eight stop watches. To whom were these distributed, and for what purpose were they purchased?
They were for the electrical branch, I understand, to be supplied to outside inspectors of electric lights.
Is there any analysis made of the cement manufactured in Canada and the cement imported into Canada from the United States?
No.

Has there been any application made to the department from the Canadian manufacturers of cement to have that done for the purpose of shutting out
cement of an inferior quality from the Unit-fc.:l States, which is sold in Canada in competition with the genuine article manufactured here?
The department has no jurisdiction in the matter, and I am informed by my deputy minister that no such request has reached the department.

All I can say is that there is a good deal of agitation throughout the country on the subject among those interested in cement factories, and I am rather surprised to hear that the department has never received any application or suggestion of that character.

Our Act refers only to
drugs, foods, and fertilizers. As cement does not fall within this classification, I do not see that the department has any authority to analyse it.

The cement industry is a growing industry in the country, and I would ask the Minister of Inland Revenue' if it is not of sufficient importance to justify some, provision being made for an analysis of this article. It will hardly do to pass it over by saying that the department has no jurisdiction, and that therefore nothing should be done.

I am informed that the Department of Public Works is making some analysis of cement for its own purposes. So far as the Department of Inland Revenue is concerned, the law provides for our analysing the three classes of articles which I have just mentioned. The question of cement has never been called to our attention.

Would it not be well to have samples of cement collected from the different cement factories throughout the country, just as you collect samples of different products, and have them brought to the chemist of the department to be analysed. to ascertain whether any of the cement is adulterated or not?

My deputy informs me that the Public Works Department does something of this kind, I do not know whether it is for its own purposes or for the public generally. My impression is that it is for its own purposes. If, however, the Department of Public Works were not doing anything in that direction, it would be worth while considering whether we should not amend our Act to make provision for analysing cement. I shall be very glad to give the question due consideration.

I am glad to hear the minister speak in the way he does of this very important industry. It is not only the manufacturers of cement who suffer because of the use of adulterated cement, but the public. Our various cities and towns use cement largely for sidewalks, and frequently you will find great cracks in some

of these sidewalks because the people laying them have been humbugged by the manufacturers of inferior cement. If there were some standard of quality imposed and a brand placed upon each barrel, the public would not be humbugged in the way they often are. I hope the minister will give this important matter his consideration.
Excise-to provide for extra duty pay at large distilleries and other factories, $7,000.

This duty pay was established by Order in Council of December 20th, 1880, and was granted on the ground that the high rates of duties charged had increased the responsibility of the officers and that the straight salaries paid them were obviously less than the qualifications necessary for the effective performance of such duties should command.
Excise-to provide for duty paid to officers serving longer hours at other than special survey, $1,000.

This is to pay deserving "officers engaged at other than the special survey, on account of their long hours of attendance and the disagreeable character of their work. They serve from 7 a.m. to 6 p. m., as they are required to be present when the factories open and close. They are simply officers in charge of the factories.
How much was expended last year ?
Have these inspectors to undergo any examination ?
Yes, they cannot be appointed unless they pass the civil service examination.
How many of these factories are there which you have to inspect and have men at all the time ?
There are nine distilleries, five tobacco factories and four or five vinegar factories.
In one item I notice you pay $7,000 for overtime of these inspectors, and you only pay them from 25 cents to 50 cents an hour overtime.

It is not a question of overtime as far as the $7,000 is concerned, but a question of special work which they do there on account of the importance to the service. It has nothing to do with the number of working hours.
You are then making no appropriation for overtime, but compel the factories to pay. If an inspector works overtime, is he paid by the factory owner or do you pay him ?
The factory owner pays the government and the government pays the officer.

Where are the particulars to be found ?
Excise-preventive service, $13,000.
How much was spent last year ?

$10,755.59. With regard to the overtime paid the inspectors, the hon. member for Lennox (Mr. Wilson) will find the particulars on page K-26 of the Auditor General's Report :	' Extra services oL
excisemen paid by manufacturers, $1,021.75.'
Excise-travelling expenses, rent, fuel and stationery, excise, $60,000.
'This covers these expenses for the entire outside branch. Last year the expenditure was $57,479.58.
Were there any prosecutions last year ?
Yes, several. There was a prosecution every time we discovered some violation of the excise law.

I presume this rent is for offices:	How many offices have you, and
where are they located ?
In all the little places in the country where the government has not got a building of its own.
In many of the smaller places you utilize the services of a customhouse officer, and he is an official of the Inland Revenue ?
Yes, and I pay him on a commission.
What commission do you pay 7
I understand about five per cent.
What does it come to in Napanee V
On page 129 of the first part of the report of the Inland Revenue Department you will find that Napanee gave $250 commission.
Has the hon. gentleman got the figures showing the expenses of rent, fuel, &c.?
No.
The vote last year was $60,000, and you are asking the same this year V
Yes.
What was the revenue last year ?
Excise-stamps for imported and Canadian tobacco, $35,000.
This is an increase of $10,000. I suppose it is for additional stamps V
Yes.
The stamps are got from the American Bank Note Company ?
Yes.
Is there a stated price for these stamps, or is there competition in the supply of them ?
There is a regular contract, which was laid before the House some years ago, fixing the amount we are to pay for these stamps.
How long was the contract for ?

It has been in existence for five years. I do not know exactly how long it has to run. The contract is not made with our department but with the Finance Department. The company is making the Dominion notes and also our stamps.
There was an over-expenditure last year under this vote. And 1 suppose the hon. gentleman expects to pay for an increased number of stamps ?

Yes, the sum expended last year was $26,000 and accounts aggregating $4,920.09 remained unpaid at the end of the fiscal year. We ask this additional vote in order to provide for that amount, and also to enable us to buy more stamps. The number of stamps required is increasing very rapidly. This year we shall collect much more revenue than before, and, consequently, shall require more stamps. Besides, of late years we have not kept a sufficiently large stock of stamps, and our intention is to provide a stock. As my hon. friend will see, if an outside officer asks for stamps and we have not them in stock to send at once, the public interest may suffer.

I suppose this is not an intimation to the dealers that the hon. gentleman proposes increasing' the duty on tobacco. It would not be a proper question for me to ask whether the hon. gentleman intends to increase the tobacco duties, because an intimation on that subject would at once be taken notice of by the trade.
I take it that there is nothing of that kind in contemplation or he would not give the trade so striking a warning just before the budget.
The increased amount has nothing to do with the tariff. And. as for the duties I cannot satisfy my hon. friend's curiosity.

If the premier assists the hon. member for Huntingdon (Mr. W. S. Maelaren) to get through his Anti-Cigarette Bill, I wonder what the effect will be on the stamps.
Excise-to pay collectors of customs allowance for duty collected by them for 1903-4, $5,500.
In soihe places, we enlist the services of the customs officers and we pay them by commission. This sum is required to pay that commission.

Do I understand that in some cases this is collected through the customs and in others through the Inland Revenue Department ? We all understand that you mean that there is a duty of fourteen cents a pound on stemmed foreign leaf coming into Canada and as customs duty of ten cents on unstemmed ; but, as a matter of convenience, and for the benefit of those who do not want to pay the duty all at once, they pay through the Inland Revenue Department as they take the tobacco out of bond. I wish to know if there are still some cases where it is collected by the customs officer ?	*
All ,the duty collected on raw leaf is collected by the Inland Revenue Department.
Although a customs duty?

No, it is not.
Mr.	CLANCY.	My	hon.	friend	(Mr. Brodeur) is mistaken. The tariff provides for that.

I think my hon. friend is misinformed. At the beginning, it was a customs duty, but afterwards the law was changed, and now it is an excise duty and is collected by the excise department.
Mr.	CLANCY.	My	hon.	friend	(Mr. Brodeur) will pardon me-that never was changed, but is part of the tariff, The method of collecting was changed, but it is a customs duty and has never become an excise duty.
According to my recollection the Customs Act states that tobacco is imported free subject to excise regulation.
No, that is the old Act.

My hon. friend will find it in section 258 of the Inland Revenue Act subsection M :-
On all foreign raw leaf tobacco, unstemmed, taken out of warehouse for manufacture in any cigar or tobacco manufactory, ten cents per pound.
Excise ?
Yes, that is the Inland Revenue Act, 60-61 Vic., chapter 19, section 13.

I am very much surprised if that is right. .
Excise-L. A. Frechette, for special translation, $100.
What is that ?

We have some circulars which are very difficult to translate on ac-

count of the technical words used, so we have to seek the services of Mr. Frechette, who is the chief translator of the House of Commons. We pay him hy the page. Last year, we paid him $95.42.
Excise-provisional allowance of not more than $100 each to officers in British Columbia whose salaries do not exceed $700 per annum, $500.

In British Columbia living is more expensive than it is in eastern Canada, and we give this additional allowance for that reason.
*
Excise-to enable the department to supply methylated spirits to manufacturers, the cost of which will be recouped by the manufacturers to whom it is supplied, and to pay for rent, light, power, freight, salaries, &c., $60,000.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Where are these spirits purchased now ?
The department buys this wood alcohol from the Standard Chemical Company, and grain alcohol is bought from the distillers.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: There has been an advance in the price to $1.40 per gallon ; is that the contract ?
There is no contract with the Standard Chemical Company ; we have to buy from them because they are the only parties producing wood alcohol in this country.
Where does this chemical company operate ?

I understand they are
operating in Deseronto, Fenelon Falls, Cookshire, and there may be a branch in Simcoe. In all these places I understand are plants operated by this company. I see by my notes that wood alcohol has been shipped from all these places I have just mentioned.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: This company then controls all the output, no matter where it is made ?
So I understand.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
And you have a contract at $1.40 per gallon.
Mr. BRODEUR, No, we have no contract.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The Postmaster General stated last year there was a contract made for the present year with these people. t
There was a contract made I think in 1898 for five years, which expired last year. But this contract has never been renewed.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Then you are continuing to pay the same price, $1.40.
Yes, that was the contract price.

How much have you purchased from them last year ?
Mr. BRODEUR, We paid them last year $16,484.44.

Would it not be the part of wisdom to ask for tenders for the supply of this article from any person who might desire to go into the manufacture, instead of giving it to one firm at their own figures, which I think are very high ?

I may say that some years ago the Rathbun Company were making wood alcohol, and we were paying them I think $1.60 a gallon. They refused to go on with the manufacture at that price, and they sold their plant to the Standard Chemical Company, all their plant producing wood alcohol. The suggestion of my hon. friend that we should ask for tenders, might be considered. It is a question whether we could get anybody to tender, because I am informed that this is the only company in this country that produces wood alcohol. We might have to go to the United States.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The government created this monopoly and established this Standard Chemical Company out in North Ontario just previous to the by-election and made a five years contract with them. Probably they forced the Rathbun Company and other manufacturers out of the business. The minister says the Rathbun Company charged $1.60. I know they charged less than $1.40, because I have been several times with Capt. Carter trying to get them to take their product. But this contract has been made, this government has created this monopoly by giving them a five years contract just previous to the election, and that shut up the Rathbun Company, they were simply forced to sell out, and this Standard Chemical Company now controls the whole industry.

I think my hon. friend is mistaken because I am informed the contract was made in 1898. It was not made with the Standard Chemical Company alone, but with the Rathbun Company also. But afterwards, I am informed, the Rathbun Company sold out all their plant to the Standard Chemical Company, and since then we have necessarily bought from the latter company because they were the only ones manufacturing wood alcohol. The Rathbun Company ceased to deliver us any goods. The contract provided that either the Rathbun Company or the Standard Chemical Company, or both combined, should, from time to time, deliver, during a period of five years, at the said price, such alcohol as the government required.
Was not this contract terminated last year ?	.
Yes.
What price do you pay this year ?
$1.40 a gallon.
Was the contract renewed without tender ?

That was the first contract we had. It was made without any tender, I think, because they were the only company making wood alcohol. I do not think there is to-day-perhaps the hon. member for South Victoria could tell us-any other company in Canada producing wood alcohol except this Standard Chemical Company.
What was the date of the existing contract ? [DOT]
No new contract has been made. We are buying to-day from the Standard Chemical Company at $1.40, but there is no contract.
Has the government ascertained the price of this commodity in the United States and what it could be imported for ?
No, we have not asked for any price in the United States. If duty had to be paid on this it would come very much above the $1.40 that is being paid today.

I have been told that it can be made and sold for less than a dollar a gallon and still leave a very large profit, and had it been open to free competition and had the government not given it all under the control of one firm, the chances are they would be getting it to-day for a much less figure than they are.

I shall be very glad to buy at a less price than that if it is possible, and if, after considering the question, I find that we are likely, if we were to ask for tenders, that we should get a better price I would be very glad. I am afraid, however, that we might not be in a better position.
Is the Rathbun Company, of DeserontO, concerned in this company V
I think so ; it is all in the Standard Chemical Company.
The Rathbun Company have leased their works at Deseronto to the Standard Company for a term of years ; it is a complicated lease.

I think there is a lawsuit over it.
Mr. POPE, The creation of wood alcohol alone, apart from the other chemicals derived from hardwood, would not be "a very profitable business. It wholly depends on the disposition that is made of the bi-products-charcoal, acetate of lime and tarproduced in the process of making wood alcohol. It is only by the sale of these that it is possible to sell at a dollar ; there is no profit in wood alcohol alone at a dollar. You have to pay for the hardwood from $4 to $5, a cord, and a cord will not produce over five gallons of wood alcohol. Consequently, without any application of labour whatever, the first cost of the wood would more than equal the selling price. It has to be solid hardwood of a certain size, and it is more expensive to cut and manufacture than the ordinary cord-wood. Consequently, you pay in the original price of the hardwood as much as you would get out ofi the wood alcohol at a dollar or one dollar and fifteen cents a gallon. So that the price at which the minister may be able to obtain it for the people of Canada is his business, not mine ; but it is a mistaken idea to think that this wood alcohol can be produced for sixty cents or seventy cents a gallon and leave a profit. Everything depends on the handling and selling of the bi-products. The sale of charcoal has been worked up by the Standard Chemical Company to a considerable extent, particularly in Montreal and Toronto. Then they export a large quantity of wood alcohol ; if they had to depend on the Canadian market the Standard Company could not carry on its business. - I have always looked upon it perhaps from a selfish standpoint, as they have an establishment in the village in which I live, in which, however, I have no interest as a shareholder. The raw material is entirely a Canadian product, the second quality of hardwood. One of the difficulties in the handling of hardwood in Canada has been that we have no market for the balance of the tree after what is known as the butt log. With this industry we are able to utilize a greater portion of the tree and get something out of it. This is of great value to the hardwood producers of Canada. The German empire, under the direct inspiration of the Emperor of Germany, has worked out a tremendous problem in the manufacture of this article. It is, I think, worthy of encouragement also from the fact that a large portion of this product is exported in addition to what is being utilized at home. At the same time we lose nothing from an economic standpoint from the extraction of the chemicals, because the charcoal has a heating power which has as much heating power as the wood before it is converted into charcoal. Consequently, I think it is a worthy industry, and personally I would feel sorry to see this article imported from the United States rather than see it manufactured in Canada. However, the minister is at liberty to see what price he can get.

My suggestion was not that it should be imported at all, but rather that an opportunity might be given to others to commence the same line of business. It is true that if you charge the whole cost to

392S
one product, the wood alcohol, you would be obliged to sell at a high rate, but then it is known that that is not the case at all. the by-products are sold to make up the difference, and when a cord of wood costs $4 or $5, when you take all the by-products into account, I am told by a party who professes to know that it could be produced and sold at less than a dollar.

There is a branch of this institution in the riding I have the honour to represent, as well as in the adjoining riding of North Ontario. Until a market was found for the charcoal and other by-products no one expected that this methylated spirits could be sold at a very low rate, but now, as the hon. member for Compton has said, there is a market for all the charcoal and more than can be produced from these industries, and, as he says, this charcoal, wihen sold, nets more than the cost of the cord of wood. With the sale of the acetate of lime and other products of the industry [DOT] the methylated spirits can be sold for 25 and 50 cents, that is if they take into account the manufacture of this charcoal and of the other commodities.
Do you know the price in the United States ?
The prioe in the United States is about one-half of the price here.

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat did not fairly state the case, in so far as the value is concerned. You get about forty-five bushels of charcoal out of a cord of wood, and this would be worth about four or five cents a bushel. Multiply these together and you get the value of the wood, to say nothing of the labour.
Might I ask when the last contract with the Standard Company expired, and also if it is anticipated that $60,000 worth of wood alcohol will be purchased this year ?
Hast year we bought only $17,000 worth.
The estimate is for $60,000 ?
We have to buy grain alcohol at the same time, and that $60,000 includes everything.
What will be the value of the wood alcohol which will be purchased this year ?
Last year it was about $17,000, and 1 suppose it will be about the same this year.
When did the contract with the Standard Company expire ?
In July, 1903.

Last year we had quite a spirited discussion upon this matter, and it was made so apparent to the Minister of Inland Revenue that he assured the House that he would not enter into another contract with this company, and that competition would be invited. It may be only a coincidence, but it is a fact, that the parties who are interested in the Standard concern at Orillia are very active Liberals. If the government of Canada wish to put up a mail contract for competition that involves an annual expenditure of perhaps a paltry $25, $8 or $10 is spent in advertising and then tenders are invited, but here the department are going to purchase probably more than $17,000 worth of an article that is made by only one firm in the country.
It is a notorious fact in that part of the country, that the Standard Chemical Company is practically owned by Liberals who are making a small fortune out of this business. Why doesn't the minister apply the healthy principle of competition, and if these people are able to supply the article as cheaply as it can be imported, let it be imported. Last year the statement was made by the member for Ottawa (Mr. Bir-kett) who is conversant with the business, that this commodity was being sold retail for $1 and $1.05 a gallon. In Orillia, where the owners of this concern are well known, there will be a feeling of suspicion that the business is not being conducted on a fair basis when the minister gives to his party friends their own price for this article.

The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Pope) has stated very concisely, the conditions under' which this industry is being canned on in Canada. The Standard Chemical Company has a large factory in the village of Longford in the riding which I represent. I happen to have some knowledge of the practical working of this industry, and I endorse what has been said by my hon. friend (Mr. Pope) as to its value to the farmers of the districts in which the different factories of the company are situated. As the hon. gentleman has well said, a class of hardwood which cannot be utilized in any other way, is utilized in this industry with great advantage to the farmers who sell that hardwood. To my own knowledge, within a radius of 100 miles of the factory in North Ontario, a class of hardwood is bought by this company which could not be utilized for any other purpose, and the farmers of that vicinity are greatly benefited in consequence thereof. I wish to know if either my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) or my hon. friend from Leeds Mr. Taylor) would rise in his place and advise the ministers to invite competition from the United States-
From the Yankees.
I for one would regret to advise the Minister of Inland Revenue to purchase wood alcohol in the United States.

The hon. member is making a suggestion which is not warranted by anything I said. If the Minister of Public Works invites competition for a building, on a public work it does not follow that he goes to the United States for contractors. There was nothing in what I said to convey the suggestion that I would invite competition by importation from the United States.

I have no wish to misrepresent my hon. friend, but it occurred to me that knowing as he did that this article is not produced in Canada except by the Standard Chemical Company, if competition is invited it must be invited from the manufacturers of this article in the United States. That would be the natural conclusion, and the only conclusion to draw from his remarks.

When the government asked for tenders for Dominion bank notes there was only one Canadian firm, but an American firm came over here and established an industry. If the government asked for tenders, and offer to contract for a reasonable length of time, for this wood alcohol it would be an invitation for.others to go into the business, as in the case of the manufacture of bank notes.

I must ask my hon. friend to stick to the question before the House. I do not think that the field for the industry is sufficiently extensive to induce others to enter into competition in the manufacture of this article. I may tell my hon. friend from East Simcoe (Mr. Bennett) that I have some knowledge of those who form the Standard Chemical Company, and that they are not altogether Liberals in polities. However, what that has to do with the question I cannot quite see.
Who are the Conservatives ?

Hon. gentlemen opposite professed to be in favour of the protection of Canadian industries, and here is an opportunity to put to the test their professions in that regard. This industry is not only important in itself, but it is of great value to the district in which the various factories are operated ; and I for one would not be disposed to advise the minister to invite competition from the United States. My hon. friend from Leeds (Mr. Taylor) made a statement which, in view of the information vouchsafed by the minister, I am sure he will retract. He said that on the eve of a by-election in North Ontario-

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I did not say by-election.

I beg the hon. gentleman's pardon. Then, he did say that on the eve of an election in North Ontario, a contract was given to this company, without tender, for the supply of this article. Now, the date of the contract as .read by the minister, is
1S98, and although my acquaintance with politics has not been very long, I do not think we had an election for some years following 1898. Therefore, the contract could not have been entered into with the view of influencing an election. More than that, the contract was not entered into, as I understand it, with the existing Standard Chemical Company, but with the Rathbun's, of Deseronto, who some years after sold out their business, and I presume that the contract then passed to the Standard Chemical Company. One hon. gentleman opposite stated that as it was now possible to sell charcoal at a considerable profit, the price of wood alcohol should be reduced. I was recently informed by a gentleman interested in this industry, that while their sales of charcoal have been considerable of late, yet, owing to reasons with which I need not weary the House, they have not been able to build up a profitable trade in charcoal, although they had every hope, that such would prove to be the case in the future. There is therefore no point in the statement that charcoal the by-product of wood alcohol being sold at a profit the price cf wood alcohol should be lessened. I regret delaying the committee at this length, but, as perhaps the largest factory belonging to this company is situated in my riding, I have a considerable interest in seeing that industry flourish, and in wishing that it should be treated at least with fairness by the government and by parliament.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Perhaps I know as much about the industry as any person in the House, from the fact that I have been associated with the Rathbun Company in business matters for a great many years. I came with Captain Carter years ago, when the hon. member for Victoria, New Brunswick (Mr. Costigan) was Minister of Inland Revenue and was importing wood alcohol from Germany. The Rathbun Company proposed to establish the industry if the government would transfer their trade to them. They agreed to do so if the price were the same and the quality equal. The Rathbun Company established the Industry, and supplied the government for years at a less price than they had paid for the imported article, and they would have continued to do so but that this government, immediately after they came into power, made a coiitract with a gentleman in Toronto for the supply, extending over a number of years.

The hon. gentleman Is mistaken.
Mi-. TAYLOR. I know better. The result was that the Rathbun Company was forced to unite with this company and afterwards sold out to it.

Then it was before
this government came into power ?

3931

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: No, it was immediately after this government came into power. They made a contract with this gentleman in Toronto for the manufacture of the product in the riding of my hou. friend. I know the way the Rathhun Company were treated by this government handing over the trade to the Toronto Chemical Com pany. If the hon. minister will advertise for tenders for the product to be made in Canada for a term of from five to ten years, he will receive tenders from half a dozen different people, notwithstanding the combine that this government has brought into being by taking the supply from the Rath-bun Company and handing it over largely to the Toronto Chemical Company.

One part of the policy of the Liberal-Conservative party is tnat whenever a combine is found to exist ir any article and to abnormally raise the price in Canada, the duty should be removed from that article, in order that the people may not suffer from the effects of the combine. I might recall the case of the salt combine formed by a number of gentlemen a few years ago in order to raise the price of salt abnormally. The Liberal-Conservative government removed the duty entirely, and that broke up the combine. There is a combine in the present case. About 50,000 gallons of methylated spirits mixed with cheap alcohol costs the government about $30,000; and yet you can buy that methylated spirits at retail at $1.50 a gallon at any drug store, showing enormous profits somewhere in that industry.

How can the hon. member for Victoria talk of combine in this matter when just a few seconds ago the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Taylor) declared that there used to be only one factory in Canada, the Rathbun, and now there is only one. Where is the difference ?

I may say that the hon. member for Leeds is mistaken so far as [DOT]the Rathbun Company is concerned. The contract made by the government was with the Rathbun Company and the Standard Chemical Company. It was signed in July, 1898. Some months afterwards the Rathbun Company wrote to the department to Mr. Miall who was then Commissioner of Inland Revenue :
We beg to advise that we have' come to an arrangement between ourselves as to the percentage ol wood alcohol you may order. In future, in order to facilitate matters, we would prefer that you send all orders to the Standard Chemical Company.
The Rathbun people themselves asked the department to send all their orders to the Standard Chemical Company.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
I would like to ask the hon. minister where this government purchased their wood alcohol during the years 1896, 1897 and 1898, up to the time that Mr. BRODEUR.
ccr.tract was entered into? I know as a n atter of fact that it was immediately after 1896, or previous to the elections of 1896, that an arrangement was made through the Postmaster General with this gentleman in Toronto to have this stuff manufactured in Orillia. It was previous to the general election that the bargain was made as to what should be done if they came in. You will find that for one or two years they purchased from this Toronto company exclusively, and left the Rathbun Company out in the cold. They afterwards forced tLe Rathbun Company to come in and join this company. I know all about it.
This government in 1896. 1897 and 1898, bought from the Rathbun people.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Partly, until their own friends manufactured enough to provide the supply.
The first sale made by the Standard Chemical Company was made in 1898.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Before this contract was made, where did the government buy it ?
I have just told the hon. gentleman that it was bought from the Rathbun people.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Not all of it.
A part of it was brought from the United States, but we thought we should discontinue that, and protect Canadian. industries.
Did he get it ?

No, because the ex-minister had a sense of fairness and could not be dragooned into giving it. No doubt the former minister was unpalatable to many for carrying on the department on that line. I know he would be to the hon. member for West York. I am glad this matter has come up, because it will show the people of that riding how this government transacts business. There was the case of a steamer belonging to the Noble Bros, concern, who were given practically a present of $25,000 through a scrape they got into with the Marine and Fisheries Department. Then there was a present to Mr. Peuchen, one of the stockholders, and Mr. Thompson, of Orillia, also a large stockholder in the concern, of this monopoly of supplying methylated spirits. The administration of the hon. gentleman will not be regarded favourably by people acquainted with these circumstances. This concern is making a huge profit by selling this wood alcohol at $1.40 per gallon, and if forced into the open market they would have to sell it for a good deal less. I am in favour of giving a preference to local industry, but I do not believe in allowing any one to hold up the government. In fact one of these gentlemen connected with that concern went on the platform in the by-election and announced that he had been- a Conservative ; but by reason of the kindly treatment accorded this institution, he saw fit to change his policy. The next week he came to Ottawa and made a request to have the contract renewed. I would ask the minister to let tenders be called for. Then if his party friends cannot supply the material as cheap as any one else, the contract should go to the lowest tender.

Last year private tenders were asked for from two or three people. They were asked from the Rathbun people, but they simply neglected to answer our letter. We asked whether they would [DOT]be prepared to supply the department with wood alcohol and they gave us no answer V A similar demand was made of the Sault people, but they were also unable to make any tender. So that the only tender we received was from the Standard Chemical Company.

Did you publicly advertise for tenders ?
Mr. 'BRODEUR. No. This is a very small amount $16,000, and it is nothing compared with the business those people are doing. The hon. member for Compton knows something about it.

I understand that the hon. member for Ontario is not in favour of tenders being asked for supplies. He says that tenders should not be asked for this amount of $17,000 worth of spirits. That applies to his own county. Would he like to see the same thing occur in any other county ?

The hon. gentleman, I am sure would not wish to misinterpret what I said, but before dealing with what I said, let me say a word or two in reply to the hon. member for East Simcoe. I had thought that the by-election in North Ontario was held so long ago and was so entirely satisfactory to the whole Dominion that we would not have it brought up now. I want to, say most emphatically that the Standard Chemical Company did not, nor did any of its officers, take an offensive part in that by-election. It is quite true that Mr. Peuchen, the president, did make a short speech, not as a Liberal, but as a Conservative. He expressly stated he was a Conservative, but that he came to North Ontario as a personal friend of mine, and gave me all the support he could. He did not canvass or interfere with his men in the slightest.
Why, it was the talk of the town, the way they were dragooned.

I wish to repeat that he did not in the slightest degree attempt to influence the votes of his workingmen. During the remarks made last session on this very question, it was stated that the subdivision of Rama township, in which the factory is located, changed its vote by giving myself a majority of forty-nine or fifty when formerly it used to give a Conservative majority of two or three. That happens to be the ease, but the change in that subdivision where this factory is situated was not as great as the change in the surrounding subdivisions of the same townships where the factory had no influence and which none of the concern even visited. The change in the subdivision of Rama is only in consonance with that in other subdivisions.

What the hon. gentleman has just said about the members of that company.not taking part in the election, he must know is not accurate. Mr. *Wm. Thompson did take a part and so did Mr. Peuchen. Mr. Geo. Thompson drove through the country.
Pardon me, he was quarantined with small-pox during the four weeks when the election was going on.
Mr. Geo. Thompson was in Muskoka and Baysville and drove through the county. I know it. He drove through with the Ontario grit government agent, named Henderson.
The hon. gentleman should take my word.
I shall not take the hon. gentleman's word, because he knows it is a matter of public notoriety.
Order.
The hon. gentleman must take the word of the hon. member.

I am not saying that he is not saying what is true, but I do not take his word. The House may take it but I will not.
Mr. B(ENNETT. I saw Mr. Geo. Thompson myself taking part in that campaign,

I want to tell the hon. gentleman that Conservatives were ordered. on pain of dismissal, to vote against the opposition candidate, but eighteen of them either spoiled their ballots or declined to vote. They said they did not wish to disobey and lose their positions and had to bow to the lash of tyranny.
What authority has the hon. gentleman for that statement ?
The authority of honest men.
Oh, oh.

They would not be coerced. He went up to these parts and used his influence for the government candidate. If he paid fair wages to his workingmen and a fair price to the farmers who supplied the wood, I would have nothing to say.
The hon. member for Compton can tell you something about that.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) if he knows the ruling prices for hard wood for this purpose ?	[DOT]	'	.
I am not subject to cross-examination
Oh, oh.

I am not subject to cross-examination by any such gentleman as the hon. member for North Ontario (Mr. Grant). We know all about the price and the workings of it ; and the intrigue and corruption in North Ontario practised by this industry.

I was under the impression that it was owing to the stuffing of ballot boxes that the Liberals had such a large majority in North Ontario. But I understand now that it was this Grit who had the small-pox running around North Ontario that frightened the Conservatives so that they did not go out to the polls. That is the explanation of the hon. gentleman's large majority. But the minister has not answered the question why he has not called for tenders for this supply.

I think the hon. gentleman (Mr. Ingram) must have heard it stated that this article is produced in Canada practically by this concern only. And advertisement for tenders would lead simply to reply from this one concern. The Minister of Inland Revenue has pointed out, and, I think he has done it well, that the amount of this contract would not be sufficient in itself to induce others to go into this industry. The public must know what is taken annually by the government, and those who contemplate going into the industry would have to estimate also what the Canadian market would require and what could be exported. It is open to anybody to enter into this manufacture and seek to sell it to the government. And there can be no doubt that if others entered into the manufacture of this article tenders would be asked for by the. department at intervals as the contract expired.
Would the minister state what is the duty on wood alcohol and when was it last increased in favour of this Standard Chemical Company-for that is the only concern benefited ?
The duty is $2.40 a gallon, imposed in 1896 or 1897. We certainly were not then making business for the Standard Chemical Company.
Has any change been made since 1S96 ? I think that came up in the discussion last year V
The hon. minister means 1897.
Yes.
And it was also brought out last year that these party friends secured not only a monopoly but an increased duty.
I said the contract was made in 1898, while the duty was fixed in 1897, the Standard Chemical Company was not in existence.

Hon. gentlemen opposite oppose reasonable protection to the industries of this country, but a concern that supplies the department with this material Is given a protection of $2.40 a gallon. 1 am sure the hon. member for North Ontario will show that he is willing to support every straggling industry by giving it reasonable protection, even though it may not be located in North Ontario.

Is there any contract for gin ? The hon. gentleman made a very notable speech not many months ago in which I find the Minister of Inland Revenue and ' the hon. member for North Ontario seem to have an affinity of views in matters of this kind. They are both what are called revenue tariff men, except on these special items, the Minister of Inland Revenue on gin, and the hon. member for North Ontario on methylated spirits. The member for North Ontario declared with no uncertain sound that it would be an outrage, a public abomination to permit the Yankees, as he called them to compete against a Canadian firm that is manufacturing spirits. Yet, he votes against everything that savours of protection. As a Canadian industry this ought to be maintained on fair grounds. But hon. gentlemen opposite are the last men who should say that competition from foreign countries should be shut out in matters of this kind. They have shown particular care of this industry. There is an interesting story about that. The person engaged in - the manufacture of this article came down and, by political pressure, succeeded in getting the present government to increase the duties on that particular article. Then followed the conversion of Mr. Peuchen to the Liberal party. I have not much doubt that he had good, substantial reason to conclude that they were the right party. And bow he has succeeded in electing the very amiable and able gentleman who represents North Ontario (Mr. Grant).
Hear, hear.

I find I am approved for once by hon. gentlemen on the other side. But I do not remember that any of these ' gentlemen, now so loud in their applause, have ever made use of any such generous expressions toward an opponent, even though it was as well deserved as in the case of the hon. .member for North Ontario. That hon. gentleman has not spoken on the tariff before. His voice has been raised to-night in favour of maintaining the privileges of this industry.

Is that the minister's ultimatum-that he does not Intend to ask for
125	'
tenders, but will go on giving this company the benefit of $1.40 a gallon or any other price they see fit to demand 7

I explained that we asked for prices from the people who should be in a position to supply wood alcohol. The Rathbun people did not even answer our letter. The Soo people could not supply us, and the only firm willing to give prices was the Standard Chemical Company. I may say, in answer to the hon. member for Both-well (Mr. Clancy), that, in 1897, the duty was raised, not only on wood alcohol, but on grain alcohol as well.
Not on all.

Yes, on all. It was not until a year later, 1898, that the Standard Chemical Company was formed and made a contract with the government. So the duty was not raised for the purpose of serving the interest of the Standard Chemical Company, for that company was not then in ex-istance.

I must congratulate Mr. Tudhope on his relations with this government. Prior to 1896 Mr. Tudhope was one of the most uncompromising Conservatives in Ontario and one of the most bitter opponents of hon. gentlemen opposite. Of course, with the change of government in 1896 he saw new light, especially when hon. gentlemen opposite increased the duties 10 percent on the cutters which he manufactured. Now, since the government are giving this company this monopoly, with the duty I have no doubt added, he will in future make some further demands on the hon. gentlemen, and the people in that part of the country will understand that all one has to do with this government is simply to be converted, and then you get what you like from them.

I notice by a Chicago trade review that wood alcohol of 95 per cent and 97 per cent sold at 65 cents a gallon.
I notice that in most of these druggists' lines there is a close similarity between American prices and Canadian prices. I am quite sure I was correct in the statement I made. The information given me was that it could be sold for $1 a gallon and afford a big profit then.
Did the hon. gentleman send out a request for tenders to any one else ?
To the Soo people, but the Soo people were not able to supply us.
Have any goods been shipped either by the Rathbun people or by the Soo people through this company the hon. gentleman is now dealing with 7

I could not say.
